title: General Embryology — question bank
note: No genuine NUST/Oman Medical College past papers are publicly available. All items are professor-written single-best-answer MCQs based on the COMHS lecture slides and Langman's Medical Embryology, 15th ed.

summary: No genuine past exam papers or MCQs from NUST Oman COMHS / Oman Medical College (or from Sultan Qaboos University) on General Embryology were found publicly indexed. Searches were run on the open web and aimed at Scribd, StuDocu, Quizlet, Telegram/Drive-indexed pages and academia.edu, using queries such as 'Oman Medical College embryology MCQ', 'NUST Oman COMHS anatomy past papers', 'Sultan Qaboos University embryology MCQ', 'studocu Oman Medical College anatomy', 'scribd Oman medical college MCQ exam' and 'quizlet Oman medical embryology'. They returned only generic or SEO-spam 'embryology MCQ' pages, generic flashcard and quiz sites with no institutional link, past-paper repositories of unrelated universities (Bowen University, Nigeria; AMREF International University, Kenya) and background pages on the institution itself. Therefore every question in this bank is professor-written from the NUST lecture slides (Dr. K. H. Afroze) and Langman's Medical Embryology 15e; no item is labelled 'past-paper' or 'regional-style', and no third-party question text was copied.

A bounded web search (8 queries, including site-restricted searches of squ.edu.om, nu.edu.om and omc.edu.om) found NO publicly available past exam questions from NUST Oman COMHS, the former Oman Medical College, or Sultan Qaboos University on the fetal period, amniotic fluid, placenta/umbilical cord, birth defects/teratology or twinning. Results were generic flashcard decks, auto-generated MCQ PDFs, research articles, and one past-paper PDF from a Nigerian university (not an Omani/Gulf institution). No Gulf-institution question was found to adapt, so all 120 items are professor-written from the lecture slides and Langman's 15e; none is labelled past-paper or regional-style.

questions.stem: In a woman with a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, where and when does fertilization most commonly occur?
options: In the isthmus of the uterine tube, around day 21
In the uterine cavity, around day 14
In the ampulla of the uterine tube, around day 14
In the infundibulum of the uterine tube, around day 7
questions.explanation: Fertilization occurs around mid-cycle (ovulation, ~day 14) in the ampulla, the widest part of the uterine tube. The uterine cavity is the site of implantation, not fertilization, and day 21 is well past the short window of oocyte viability.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Fertilization (definition, time, site) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Fertilization is best defined as:
options: Embedding of the blastocyst in the functional endometrium
Removal of proteins from the plasma membrane over the sperm head
Mitotic division of the zygote into smaller blastomeres
Fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to form a zygote
questions.explanation: Fertilization is the fusion of spermatozoon and oocyte producing the zygote. The other options define implantation, capacitation and cleavage respectively - classic look-alike terms.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Fertilization definition slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: All of the following are prerequisites that must occur BEFORE fertilization EXCEPT:
options: Capacitation of spermatozoa
Acrosome reaction
Transport of sperm and oocyte to the ampulla
Cortical and zona reactions
questions.explanation: The lecture lists three prerequisites: gamete transport, capacitation and the acrosome reaction. The cortical and zona reactions are consequences of fertilization, triggered after the first sperm fuses with the oocyte, to block polyspermy.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Prerequisites slide and Results of fertilization slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: A woman has extensive loss of the ciliated epithelium of her uterine tubes after a pelvic infection. Which process involved in fertilization is MOST directly impaired?
options: Release of hyaluronidase from the sperm acrosome
Transport of the oocyte toward the ampulla
Completion of meiosis I by the oocyte
The zona reaction after sperm entry
questions.explanation: Oocyte transport depends on fluid currents produced by tubal cilia together with peristalsis of the tube, which sweep the oocyte toward the ampulla. Hyaluronidase release is a sperm (acrosomal) event, and meiosis I is completed before ovulation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Oocyte transport slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: In the male, the main storage site of spermatozoa before ejaculation is the:
options: Tail of the epididymis
Seminiferous tubules
Seminal vesicle
Prostatic urethra
questions.explanation: Sperm are stored mainly in the tail of the epididymis and are propelled by peristaltic contractions of the vas deferens into the urethra. Despite the name, seminal vesicles secrete seminal fluid and are not the storage site.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Sperm transport (in male) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: During intercourse, approximately how many spermatozoa are ejaculated, where are they deposited, and why do many die there?
options: 2-6 million; cervical canal; cervical mucus enzymes
200-600 million; posterior fornix of the vagina; vaginal acidity
20-60 million; uterine cavity; phagocytosis by endometrial cells
2-6 billion; anterior fornix of the vagina; alkaline seminal fluid
questions.explanation: Per the lecture, 200-600 million sperm are deposited in the posterior fornix, and many die because of the acidity of the vagina (Langman quotes 200-300 million, which lies within this range). Cervical mucus slows sperm in the cervix but is not the site of deposition.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Sperm transport (in female) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes sperm transport through the female genital tract?
options: Through the cervix by uterine contractions alone; through the uterine tube solely by their own tail movements against the current
Through the cervix and uterus passively in cervical mucus; to the ampulla by the same ciliary currents that carry the oocyte
Through the cervix rapidly because cervical mucus accelerates them; through the tubes by peristalsis of the vas deferens
Through the cervix by their own tail movements (slowed by mucus); through the uterus and tubes mainly by muscular contractions of the tract
questions.explanation: The lecture states sperm traverse the cervix by tail movements (slowly, because of cervical mucus) and move through the uterus and tubes by muscular contractions of these organs. Tubal ciliary currents are directed toward the uterus to carry the oocyte, so they do not carry sperm to the ampulla.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Sperm transport (in female) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Of the hundreds of millions of spermatozoa deposited in the vagina, approximately how many reach the ampulla (site of fertilization)?
options: Only one
Only a few hundred
About 2-3 million
About 100 million
questions.explanation: Only a few hundred sperm reach the ampulla (lecture: about 200; Langman: 300-500), and only one of them fertilizes the oocyte. 'Only one' describes the number that fertilizes, not the number that arrives.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Sperm transport (Fate) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: According to the lecture, after deposition in the female genital tract spermatozoa retain their fertilizing power for approximately:
options: 30 minutes
2-5 days
2-3 weeks
2-3 months
questions.explanation: The lecture states the fertilizing power of sperm lasts 2-5 days, which is why intercourse several days before ovulation can still result in pregnancy. Thirty minutes is closer to the fastest transit time, not the survival time.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Sperm transport slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Capacitation of spermatozoa is best described as:
options: Removal of proteins from the plasma membrane over the sperm head, over about 5-7 hours in the female tract
Release of hyaluronidase and acrosin from the acrosome when the sperm reaches the coats of the oocyte
Transformation of round spermatids into motile spermatozoa within the seminiferous tubules of the testis
Hardening of the zona pellucida by cortical granule enzymes after entry of the first spermatozoon
questions.explanation: Capacitation is removal of proteins from the plasma membrane over the sperm head; it lasts about 5-7 hours (Langman: about 7 hours) and makes sperm more active and able to fertilize. Enzyme release from the acrosome is the acrosome reaction, which can only follow capacitation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Capacitation slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: In an IVF laboratory, freshly ejaculated sperm placed directly with oocytes fail to fertilize unless they are first incubated in a special medium for several hours. This incubation is required because only sperm that have undergone which process can undergo the acrosome reaction and fertilize?
options: Spermiogenesis
Cortical reaction
Compaction
Capacitation
questions.explanation: Only capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction and fertilize; in vivo capacitation takes 5-7 hours in the female tract, so in IVF it must be reproduced in culture. Spermiogenesis is completed in the testis before ejaculation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Capacitation and Acrosomal reaction slides (NB: only capacitated sperm undergo acrosome reaction); Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: During the acrosome reaction, which occurs in the vicinity of the oocyte, which acrosomal enzyme mainly enables the sperm to penetrate the corona radiata?
options: Hyaluronidase
Acrosin (zona lysin)
Trypsin-like substances
Cortical granule enzymes
questions.explanation: The lecture lists hyaluronidase as the enzyme that penetrates the corona radiata. Acrosin (zona lysin) and trypsin-like substances act on the zona pellucida, and cortical granules belong to the oocyte, not the sperm.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Acrosomal reaction slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Acrosin (zona lysin) and trypsin-like substances released during the acrosome reaction act mainly on the:
options: Corona radiata
Zona pellucida
Oocyte plasma membrane
Theca interna of the follicle
questions.explanation: Trypsin-like substances digest, and acrosin/zona lysin softens, the zona pellucida so the sperm can reach the oocyte membrane. The corona radiata is penetrated mainly with the help of hyaluronidase.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Acrosomal reaction slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Which group of factors helps spermatozoa pass through the corona radiata (phase 1 of fertilization)?
options: Acrosin, trypsin-like enzymes and cortical granule enzymes of the oocyte
Acrosomal hyaluronidase, tubal mucosal enzymes and sperm tail movements
Uterine muscle contractions, cervical mucus and vaginal acidity
Progesterone, hCG and oestrogen secreted by the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (penetration of the corona radiata) is assisted by acrosomal hyaluronidase, tubal mucosal enzymes and sperm tail movements. Acrosin and the zona reaction belong to phase 2, penetration of the zona pellucida.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Penetration of corona radiata) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Once the first spermatozoon has penetrated, the zona pellucida alters its composition and becomes impermeable to other sperm. The main significance of this zona reaction is:
options: Initiation of capacitation
Prevention of polyspermy
Triggering of the acrosome reaction in other sperm
Prevention of implantation in the uterine tube
questions.explanation: The zona reaction makes the zona impermeable to additional sperm and is the main block to polyspermy. The (intact) zona does also prevent premature adhesion in the tube, but that is a property of its presence during transport, not the purpose of the zona reaction.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Penetration of zona pellucida) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Immediately after sperm-oocyte fusion, a rise in intracellular calcium in the oocyte triggers a reaction that blocks polyspermy. Which sequence correctly describes this cortical reaction?
options: Cortical granule exocytosis -> enzymes alter zona glycoproteins (sperm receptors) -> zona hardens
Hyaluronidase release by the oocyte -> corona radiata disperses -> other sperm are washed away
Completion of meiosis I -> first polar body is extruded -> zona pellucida closes over the oocyte
Sperm plasma membrane is shed -> male pronucleus forms -> pronuclei fuse to form the zygote
questions.explanation: Fusion raises oocyte Ca2+, causing cortical granule exocytosis; the released enzymes alter zona glycoproteins/ZP receptors so the zona hardens (zona reaction), blocking polyspermy. Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, so it cannot be the response to sperm entry.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Cortical reaction slide figure and Results of fertilization slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: When the plasma membranes of the sperm and the secondary oocyte fuse, which part(s) of the spermatozoon enter the oocyte cytoplasm?
options: Head and tail; the sperm plasma membrane stays behind
Only the head; the tail stays outside the zona pellucida
Only the acrosome and nucleus; the midpiece is shed
The entire sperm, including its plasma membrane
questions.explanation: In humans both head and tail enter the oocyte cytoplasm, while the sperm plasma membrane is left behind on the oocyte surface. The tail then degenerates as the male pronucleus forms.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Fusion of plasma membranes) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Entry of the sperm into the secondary oocyte (activation of the oocyte) immediately causes the oocyte to:
options: Complete meiosis I, forming the secondary oocyte and the first polar body
Complete meiosis II, forming the mature ovum and the second polar body
Begin cleavage immediately, producing two equal-sized blastomeres
Undergo capacitation, removing proteins from its plasma membrane
questions.explanation: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested in meiosis II and completes it only after sperm entry, producing the mature ovum (female pronucleus) and the second polar body. Meiosis I and the first polar body are completed before ovulation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Activation of oocyte) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: The female pronucleus formed after completion of meiosis II contains:
options: 46 chromosomes: 44 autosomes plus XX
23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes plus either an X or a Y chromosome
22 chromosomes with no sex chromosome
23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes plus an X chromosome
questions.explanation: The female pronucleus is haploid with 22 autosomes + X (written on the slide as '22,X', i.e. 23 chromosomes in total). '22 autosomes plus X or Y' describes the male pronucleus, because only sperm can carry a Y.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Activation of oocyte; Male pronucleus) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: An oocyte containing two haploid pronuclei (male and female) before they fuse is termed the:
options: Ootid
Zygote
Morula
Blastomere
questions.explanation: The lecture names the oocyte containing two haploid pronuclei the ootid; it is called a zygote only when the pronuclei come together into a single diploid set. Blastomeres and the morula arise later, during cleavage.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Formation of male pronucleus) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Which event occurs in the male and female pronuclei before they come together to form the zygote?
options: Each undergoes a further reduction (meiotic) division
The male pronucleus discards its X or Y chromosome
Crossing over occurs between maternal and paternal sets
Each replicates its DNA (two chromatids per chromosome)
questions.explanation: Both haploid pronuclei replicate their DNA before fusion, so each centromere carries two chromatids, ready for the first cleavage division. Reduction division and crossing over take place earlier, during gametogenesis (meiosis), not in the pronuclei.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Phases of fertilization (Fusion of pronuclei) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: A couple asks when and how the sex of their baby is determined. The chromosomal sex of the embryo is determined at:
options: Fertilization, depending on whether the oocyte carries an X or a Y chromosome
Implantation, depending on the hormonal environment of the endometrium
Fertilization, depending on whether the fertilizing sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome
Gastrulation, depending on signals from the primitive streak
questions.explanation: Sex is determined at fertilization: an X-bearing sperm produces a female (XX) and a Y-bearing sperm a male (XY). The oocyte always contributes an X chromosome, so it cannot determine sex.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Results of fertilization (Sex of the baby) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Which is a direct result (consequence) of fertilization?
options: Completion of the first meiotic division of the oocyte
Capacitation of the spermatozoon that fertilizes the oocyte
Restoration of the diploid number (46) of chromosomes
Formation of the corona radiata around the oocyte
questions.explanation: Results of fertilization include completion of meiosis II, the cortical/zona reaction, restoration of 46 chromosomes, sex determination, variation by shuffling of parental chromosomes and initiation of cleavage. Capacitation is a prerequisite, not a result, and meiosis I is completed before ovulation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Results (effects/consequences) of fertilization slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: A woman delivers dizygotic twins. DNA testing shows that the twins have different biological fathers. Both oocytes were released during the same menstrual cycle. This phenomenon is called:
options: Superfetation
Polyspermy
Superfecundation
Parthenogenesis
questions.explanation: Superfecundation is fertilization of two or more ova released in the same cycle by sperm from separate acts of coitus (same or different males). If the ova come from different cycles it is superfetation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Abnormal fertilization (Superfecundation) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Karyotyping of a spontaneously aborted conceptus shows 69,XXY. Which abnormal fertilization event most likely explains this?
options: Superfecundation
Parthenogenesis
Superfetation
Polyspermy
questions.explanation: Fertilization of one oocyte by two sperm (polyspermy/dispermy) adds an extra haploid set, giving a triploid (3n = 69) zygote such as 69,XXY, which is usually lost early. Superfecundation produces two separate, normal diploid zygotes.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Abnormal fertilization (Polyspermia) slide and figure (triploid 69,XXY); Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Development of an embryo from an unfertilized oocyte, without any contribution from a male gamete, is termed:
options: Parthenogenesis
Superfetation
Capacitation
Superfecundation
questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis ('virgin birth') is cleavage of an unfertilized oocyte to give a growing embryo; it occurs naturally in plants, some invertebrates and fish. Superfetation and superfecundation both require fertilization.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Abnormal fertilization (Parthenogenesis) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Which statement about cleavage of the zygote is correct?
options: It starts within about 30 hours in the uterine tube; blastomeres get smaller inside the intact zona pellucida
It starts only after the zygote reaches the uterine cavity, once the zona pellucida has been shed
It starts within about 30 hours, and the conceptus enlarges because blastomeres keep their original size
It starts in the ampulla after the zona pellucida disappears at the 2-cell stage to permit division
questions.explanation: Cleavage (onset of mitosis in the zygote) starts within ~30 hours, occurs in the uterine tube over the first 3 days, and produces progressively smaller blastomeres inside the intact zona pellucida. The zona persists until about day 5-6, just before implantation.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Cleavage slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Approximately 3 days after fertilization, the conceptus consists of about 16 blastomeres and resembles a mulberry. It is called the:
options: Blastocyst
Zygote
Morula
Bilaminar germ disc
questions.explanation: The 16-cell stage is the morula, present about 3 days after fertilization around the time it reaches the uterus (Langman: enters the uterine cavity at ~day 4). The blastocyst forms only after fluid enters the morula.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Cleavage / Morula slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Formation of the blastocyst begins when:
options: Fluid secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast accumulates between epiblast and trophoblast as the amniotic cavity
The zona pellucida ruptures and maternal blood from eroded sinusoids enters the centre of the morula
Uterine fluid passes through the zona pellucida into the morula and the spaces coalesce into the blastocoel
Hypoblast cells spread to line the cavity of the morula, forming Heuser's membrane and the yolk sac
questions.explanation: Shortly after the morula reaches the uterus, uterine fluid passes through the zona into it; the spaces coalesce to form the blastocoel, and the whole structure is the blastocyst. Heuser's membrane and the amniotic cavity form later, in week 2.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Blastocyst slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: As fluid accumulates in the blastocyst, the inner cell mass is pushed to one pole. Which pairing is correct?
options: Embryoblast at the abembryonic pole forms the placenta; trophoblast at the embryonic pole forms the embryo
Trophoblast forms the embryo proper; embryoblast forms only the chorion and the amnion of the conceptus
Embryoblast at the embryonic pole forms the embryo; trophoblast forms the fetal part of the placenta
Embryoblast forms the maternal decidua; trophoblast forms the amnion and the umbilical cord of the embryo
questions.explanation: The inner cell mass (embryoblast) lies eccentrically at the embryonic pole and forms the embryo, while the flattened outer trophoblast forms the fetal part of the placenta. The opposite side is the abembryonic pole; the decidua is maternal endometrium.
questions.source: Lecture: Fertilization & First Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Blastocyst slides (embryo pole, trophoblast, embryoblast); Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: During the second week, embryoblast cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity become small and cuboidal. This layer is the:
options: Epiblast
Cytotrophoblast
Hypoblast
Syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: Embryoblast cells facing the blastocyst cavity become the cuboidal hypoblast, whereas those toward the embryonic pole (future amniotic cavity) become the columnar epiblast. Together they form the bilaminar germ disc.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Bilaminar germ disc slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: Which layer of the bilaminar germ disc is the source of all three definitive germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm)?
options: Hypoblast
Epiblast
Extraembryonic mesoderm
Cytotrophoblast
questions.explanation: All three germ layers derive from the epiblast: during gastrulation, invaginating epiblast cells displace the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm. So the hypoblast is not the definitive endoderm, even though the week-2 slide labels it '(Endoderm)'.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Bilaminar germ disc slide; Lecture: Third Week of Development - Gastrulation slide ('all three germ layers are derived from epiblast'); Langman's 15e Ch.4-5

questions.stem: The amniotic cavity is lined by amnioblasts. From which layer do the amnioblasts arise, and what forms the floor of the amniotic cavity?
options: Amnioblasts arise from the hypoblast, and the hypoblast forms the floor
Amnioblasts arise from the epiblast, and the epiblast forms the floor
Amnioblasts arise from the cytotrophoblast, and the epiblast forms the floor
Amnioblasts arise from extraembryonic mesoderm, and Heuser's membrane forms the floor
questions.explanation: Amnioblasts differentiate from the epiblast and line the amniotic cavity, while the epiblast itself forms its floor. The hypoblast faces the opposite cavity (primary yolk sac).
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of amniotic cavity slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: The definitive amnion (amniotic membrane) is composed of:
options: Trophoblast plus extraembryonic somatic mesoderm
Hypoblast plus extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm
Epiblast and hypoblast of the bilaminar disc
Amnioblasts plus extraembryonic somatic mesoderm
questions.explanation: The amnion consists of amniotic cells (amnioblasts) plus somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. Trophoblast plus somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm forms the chorion instead.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Chorion and Amnion slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: Hypoblast-derived cells proliferate and line the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast as a thin membrane. This membrane is the:
options: Amniotic membrane
Chorionic plate
Heuser's membrane
Buccopharyngeal membrane
questions.explanation: Hypoblast cells spread to line the blastocyst cavity as Heuser's (exocoelomic) membrane, converting the cavity into the primary yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity). The buccopharyngeal membrane forms in week 3 from ectoderm and endoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of primary yolk sac slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: The terms 'exocoelomic cavity' and 'extraembryonic coelom' are easily confused. The exocoelomic cavity is another name for the ___, whereas the extraembryonic coelom is also called the ___.
options: chorionic cavity; primary yolk sac
amniotic cavity; blastocoel
secondary yolk sac; amniotic cavity
primary yolk sac; chorionic cavity
questions.explanation: The blastocyst cavity lined by Heuser's membrane is the primary yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity). Spaces that coalesce within the extraembryonic mesoderm form the extraembryonic coelom, which is the chorionic cavity.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Primary yolk sac slide and Extraembryonic coelomic cavity slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the two layers of the trophoblast during the second week?
options: Inner syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated mass; outer cytotrophoblast of distinct, mitotically active cells
Both layers are multinucleated syncytia without cell boundaries that invade the endometrium together
Inner cytotrophoblast forms the amnion; outer syncytiotrophoblast forms the wall of the primary yolk sac
Inner cytotrophoblast of distinct cells; outer syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated mass without cell boundaries
questions.explanation: The trophoblast differentiates into an inner cytotrophoblast of distinct cells and an outer syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated protoplasmic mass whose cells have lost their membranes. The common error is reversing inner and outer.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Changes in trophoblast slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: A woman's urine pregnancy test becomes positive at about the end of the second week after fertilization. The hormone detected, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), is produced by the:
options: Syncytiotrophoblast
Cytotrophoblast
Decidua basalis
Hypoblast
questions.explanation: Langman: the syncytiotrophoblast produces hCG, and by the end of week 2 levels are high enough for pregnancy tests. The cytotrophoblast is the mitotically active layer that feeds cells into the syncytium but is not the main hormone source.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Trophoblast slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Implantation (the embedding of the blastocyst in the functional endometrium) begins and is completed at approximately which times after fertilization?
options: Begins day 1; completed by day 3
Begins day 5-6; completed by day 11-12
Begins day 14; completed by day 21
Begins day 3; completed by day 5
questions.explanation: Implantation begins at the end of the first week (day 5-6) and is completed by the end of the second week (day 11-12). Days 1-3 are occupied by cleavage in the uterine tube.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Implantation (definition, time) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3-4

questions.stem: The most common normal site of implantation, as described in the lecture, is the:
options: Upper posterior wall of the uterine body, near the fundus
Lower uterine segment, close to the internal os
Ampulla of the uterine tube, near the infundibulum
Cervical canal, just below the internal os
questions.explanation: Normal implantation occurs in the upper part of the body of the uterus near the fundus (the lecture specifies the posterior wall; Langman says anterior or posterior wall). Implantation in the lower segment near the internal os produces placenta previa.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Implantation (site) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: The zona pellucida normally persists until the conceptus reaches the uterine cavity and then degenerates (around day 5-6). If the zona pellucida disappeared prematurely while the conceptus was still in the uterine tube, the most likely consequence would be:
options: Tubal ectopic pregnancy
Failure of capacitation
Placenta previa
Polyspermy
questions.explanation: The zona pellucida prevents the embryo from sticking to the uterine tube until it reaches the uterine cavity; premature loss exposes the adhesive trophoblast in the tube. Polyspermy is a fertilization event that has already been prevented by the zona reaction.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Steps of implantation slide (NOTE on zona pellucida); Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: At the start of implantation, which cells send finger-like processes into the uterine endometrium and burrow into it?
options: Cytotrophoblast at the abembryonic pole
Hypoblast at the embryonic pole
Syncytiotrophoblast at the embryonic pole
Epiblast at the abembryonic pole
questions.explanation: Numerous finger-like processes of the syncytiotrophoblast at the embryonic pole invade and burrow into the endometrium. The cytotrophoblast lies internal to it and does not lead the invasion; the hypoblast and epiblast are embryoblast layers.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Steps of implantation slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3-4

questions.stem: The decidua is best defined as:
options: Myometrium of the pregnant uterus, stimulated by oestrogen
Fetal part of the placenta, derived from the trophoblast
Endometrium of the pregnant uterus, maintained by progesterone
Extraembryonic mesoderm lining the chorionic cavity
questions.explanation: The decidua is the endometrium of pregnancy; it has secretory-phase structure, is maintained by progesterone, and supports the pregnancy. The fetal part of the placenta comes from the trophoblast, not the decidua.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Decidua (definition, structure, control) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: The part of the decidua lying between the implanted conceptus and the myometrium is the:
options: Decidua capsularis
Decidua parietalis
Decidua basalis
Chorion laeve
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus, between it and the myometrium. The decidua capsularis covers the conceptus on its luminal side, and the chorion laeve is a fetal membrane.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Decidua (parts) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches the decidua that covers the implanted conceptus on its luminal side and the decidua that lines the rest of the uterine cavity?
options: Decidua parietalis; decidua capsularis
Decidua basalis; decidua capsularis
Decidua basalis; decidua parietalis
Decidua capsularis; decidua parietalis
questions.explanation: The decidua capsularis covers the conceptus, and the decidua parietalis lines the remainder of the uterine cavity. The decidua basalis lies between the conceptus and the myometrium.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Decidua (parts) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which part of the decidua enlarges to form the maternal part of the placenta?
options: Decidua capsularis
Decidua parietalis
Fused decidua capsularis and parietalis
Decidua basalis
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis enlarges to form the maternal component of the placenta. The capsularis and parietalis fuse and then degenerate, so they do not form placenta.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Decidua (fate) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: As the gestational sac enlarges, what is the fate of the decidua capsularis and decidua parietalis?
options: They form the maternal part of the placenta
They fuse with each other and then degenerate, obliterating the uterine cavity
They form the umbilical cord
They remain as separate layers lining an open uterine cavity until delivery
questions.explanation: The enlarging conceptus pushes the decidua capsularis against the decidua parietalis; they fuse and degenerate, obliterating the uterine lumen. Only the decidua basalis forms the maternal placenta.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Decidua (fate) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks' gestation presents with sudden, painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the placenta lying in the lower uterine segment. This condition results from:
options: Implantation of the blastocyst in the lower uterine segment
Implantation of the blastocyst in the ampulla of the tube
Implantation in the upper posterior wall of the uterine body
Premature separation of a normally situated placenta
questions.explanation: Placenta previa is due to implantation of the blastocyst in the inferior uterine segment, near or over the internal os; it causes bleeding in the second half of pregnancy and at delivery. Premature separation of a normally sited placenta is abruption, which is typically painful.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Abnormal implantation: Placenta previa slide; Langman's 15e Ch.3 & Ch.8

questions.stem: Ultrasound shows a placenta that completely covers the internal os. This type of placenta previa is:
options: Placenta previa marginalis
Placenta previa centralis
Placenta previa partialis
Placenta previa lateralis
questions.explanation: Centralis (complete) placenta previa completely covers the internal os. Partialis covers it only partly, marginalis reaches its edge, and lateralis lies in the lower segment without reaching it.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Placenta previa (types) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: In which type of placenta previa does the placental edge reach (touch) the internal os without covering the opening?
options: Lateralis
Marginalis
Partialis
Centralis
questions.explanation: In placenta previa marginalis, the edge touches the internal os without covering it. Partialis covers part of the os, and lateralis lies in the lower segment but does not reach the os.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Placenta previa (types) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment that does not reach (is not related to) the internal os is classified as placenta previa:
options: Lateralis
Marginalis
Partialis
Centralis
questions.explanation: Placenta previa lateralis lies in the lower segment but is not related to the internal os. Once the edge touches the os it becomes marginalis.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Placenta previa (types) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea and a positive pregnancy test develops sudden right-sided lower abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity. The single most likely site of this ectopic implantation is the:
options: Isthmus of the uterine tube
Ampulla of the uterine tube
Ovary
Cervix
questions.explanation: About 95% of ectopic pregnancies are tubal, and the ampulla is the commonest tubal site (slide figure: ~70%; Langman: ~80%), followed by the isthmus (~12%). Typically there are early signs of pregnancy followed by pain on one side.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Ectopic pregnancies slide and ectopic-site slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.3 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of all ectopic pregnancies occur in the uterine tube?
options: About 3%
About 50%
About 70%
About 95%
questions.explanation: Tubal pregnancy is the most common ectopic pregnancy, about 95% of the total. The 70% figure on the slide refers to the ampullary portion of tubal pregnancies, and ~3% is the share for ovarian pregnancy.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Ectopic pregnancies slide (tubal 95%) and ectopic-site slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: A secondary ovarian pregnancy is one in which:
options: The blastocyst implants directly on the ovarian surface after ovulation
Two ova from the same ovary are fertilized during the same cycle
The conceptus re-implants on the ovary after a tubal pregnancy ruptures
The placenta grows from the uterus to attach secondarily to the ovary
questions.explanation: Primary ovarian pregnancy is direct implantation on the ovary; secondary ovarian pregnancy is re-implantation on the ovary after a tubal pregnancy ruptures. Ovarian pregnancies make up only about 3% of ectopics; cervical and caesarean-scar pregnancies are each under 1%.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Ectopic pregnancies (ovarian) slide and ectopic-site slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: At laparotomy, a conceptus is found implanted on the peritoneum of the rectouterine pouch, with normal uterine tubes and ovaries. This is best classified as:
options: Primary ovarian pregnancy
Placenta previa centralis
Tubal pregnancy
Abdominal pregnancy
questions.explanation: Implantation on peritoneum or the surface of abdominal viscera is an abdominal (peritoneal) pregnancy; Langman notes the rectouterine (Douglas) pouch is its most frequent site. It is rare (~1%, grouped with intraligamentous on the slide figure).
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Ectopic pregnancies (abdominal) slide and slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.3

questions.stem: Extraembryonic mesoderm first appears as a loose tissue located between:
options: The cytotrophoblast and the primary yolk sac
The epiblast and the hypoblast of the disc
The syncytiotrophoblast and the endometrium
The cytotrophoblast and the syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: A new population of cells, the extraembryonic mesoderm, forms between the cytotrophoblast and the primary yolk sac (exocoelomic membrane) and separates the amnion and yolk sac from the trophoblast. Intraembryonic mesoderm between epiblast and hypoblast appears only in week 3.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Extraembryonic mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: Spaces in the extraembryonic mesoderm coalesce to form the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity). The layer of extraembryonic mesoderm that lines the cytotrophoblast and covers the amnion is the:
options: Extraembryonic splanchnic (splanchnopleuric) mesoderm
Intraembryonic paraxial mesoderm
Exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane
Extraembryonic somatic (somatopleuric) mesoderm
questions.explanation: Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm lines the trophoblast and covers the amnion, whereas extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the yolk sac. The two layers are continuous only at the connecting stalk.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Extraembryonic coelomic cavity slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: The only site where extraembryonic mesoderm crosses the chorionic cavity, attaching the caudal end of the embryo to the trophoblast, is the ___, which later forms the umbilical cord.
options: Connecting stalk
Vitelline duct
Allantois
Chorionic plate
questions.explanation: The somatic and splanchnic layers of extraembryonic mesoderm meet at the caudal end of the embryo in the connecting stalk, the forerunner of the umbilical cord. The vitelline duct is the later connection between midgut and yolk sac.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Extraembryonic coelomic cavity slide (connecting stalk); Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: The chorion is formed by:
options: Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm plus amnioblasts
Extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm plus hypoblast
Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm plus trophoblast
Decidua basalis plus syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: The chorion is somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm plus the trophoblast, and it lines the chorionic cavity. Somatopleuric mesoderm plus amnioblasts forms the amnion, and the decidua is maternal tissue.
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Chorion and Amnion slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: By about days 11-12, the uteroplacental circulation is established when:
options: Cytotrophoblast invades the umbilical arteries, and fetal blood enters the lacunae
The embryonic heart begins to pump fetal blood into the chorionic villi
Syncytiotrophoblast erodes maternal sinusoids, and maternal blood enters the lacunae
Extraembryonic mesoderm forms vessels that drain directly into uterine veins
questions.explanation: Langman: syncytiotrophoblast penetrates deeper into the stroma and erodes maternal sinusoids, and the lacunae become continuous with them, so maternal blood enters the lacunar system. The embryonic heart does not beat until the 4th week (around day 21-22).
questions.source: Lecture: Implantation & Second Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - SLO 6 (uteroplacental circulation); Langman's 15e Ch.4

questions.stem: At about day 14, while the embryo is still a bilaminar disc, a localized area of hypoblast cells becomes columnar, forming a thickened circular plate that marks the future head (cranial) end. This structure is the:
options: Primitive node
Neural plate
Cloacal membrane
Prechordal plate
questions.explanation: The prechordal plate is a localized columnar thickening of the hypoblast that indicates the future head end and helps define the central axis. The primitive node lies at the cranial end of the primitive streak, which itself marks the caudal region.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Prechordal plate slide; Langman's 15e Ch.4-5

questions.stem: The primitive streak is formed by:
options: Epiblast cells proliferating and migrating to the midline at the caudal end
Hypoblast cells proliferating at the cranial end of the embryonic disc
Cytotrophoblast cells thickening at the embryonic pole of the blastocyst
Extraembryonic mesoderm condensing within the connecting stalk
questions.explanation: Epiblast cells at the tail end proliferate and migrate toward the median plane, forming the primitive streak as a caudal midline thickening. The cranial-end hypoblast thickening is the prechordal plate, not the streak.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Primitive streak slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: A woman drank a large amount of alcohol at a party about 4 weeks after her last menstrual period, before she knew she was pregnant. Her baby is born with a small forebrain, a single fused lateral ventricle and closely set eyes (hypotelorism). The most likely explanation is:
options: Anencephaly due to failure of cranial neuropore closure on day 25
Holoprosencephaly due to loss of anterior midline cells at gastrulation
Caudal dysgenesis due to insufficient mesoderm in the caudal region
Sacrococcygeal teratoma due to persistence of the primitive streak
questions.explanation: Gastrulation, about 2 weeks after fertilization (about 4 weeks after the LMP), is very sensitive to teratogens. High-dose alcohol kills anterior midline cells, producing holoprosencephaly with a small forebrain, a single ventricle and hypotelorism. Anencephaly is a failure of neural tube closure, not a midline cell-loss defect.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Self-study page (Langman text: teratogenesis associated with gastrulation); Langman's 15e Ch.5 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the primitive node, primitive pit and primitive groove?
options: The node is a swelling at the caudal end of the streak; the pit is a depression in the prechordal plate
The pit and groove are cavities within the hypoblast that enlarge to become the primary yolk sac
The node forms the notochord directly; the pit forms the oral opening and the groove forms the anus
The node is a swelling at the cranial end of the streak; the pit is a depression in the node that continues as the groove
questions.explanation: Cells at the cranial end of the streak form the primitive node (knot); its depression is the primitive pit (called 'blastopore' on the slide), which continues into the streak as the primitive groove. The oral and anal openings come from the buccopharyngeal and cloacal membranes.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Primitive streak / node / pit slides; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Appearance of the primitive streak is significant mainly because it allows identification of:
options: The cranio-caudal axis and the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the embryo
Only the site of the future umbilical cord and connecting stalk
The site of implantation on the posterior uterine wall
The future position of the placenta on the uterine wall
questions.explanation: The primitive streak and groove establish the central axis and the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the embryonic disc, so the cranial/caudal ends and the right/left sides can be identified (Langman). It does not determine the implantation or placental site.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Primitive streak (pit/groove) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Epiblast cells that reach the primitive groove become flask-shaped, detach and invaginate between the epiblast and hypoblast, converting the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar germ disc. This process is called:
options: Gastrulation
Neurulation
Cleavage
Compaction
questions.explanation: Gastrulation is the invagination of epiblast cells through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers (trilaminar disc). Neurulation, the formation of the neural tube, follows later and is induced by the notochord.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gastrulation slides; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: During gastrulation, some invaginating epiblast cells displace (replace) the hypoblast. These cells form the:
options: Intraembryonic mesoderm
Embryonic ectoderm
Definitive endoderm
Extraembryonic mesoderm
questions.explanation: Invaginating epiblast cells that replace the hypoblast become the definitive (embryonic) endoderm; those spreading between epiblast and the new endoderm form intraembryonic mesoderm, and cells remaining in the epiblast become ectoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gastrulation slides; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: In an experiment, all epiblast cells of an embryo are labelled with a permanent dye on day 13. At the end of the third week, the label would be found in the:
options: Ectoderm only
Ectoderm, intraembryonic mesoderm and embryonic endoderm
Ectoderm and mesoderm only, because endoderm comes from the hypoblast
Endoderm only
questions.explanation: All three germ layers arise ultimately from the epiblast, so labelled epiblast gives labelled ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. The idea that endoderm comes from hypoblast is the classic misconception; the hypoblast is displaced.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gastrulation slide ('all three germ layers are derived from epiblast'); Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: An infant of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes is born with fused lower limbs (sirenomelia), vertebral anomalies, renal agenesis, imperforate anus and genital anomalies. This caudal dysgenesis results from:
options: Insufficient formation of mesoderm in the caudal-most region of the embryo
Failure of the cranial neuropore to close
Persistence of remnants of the primitive streak forming a tumour
Failure of the decidua capsularis to fuse with the decidua parietalis
questions.explanation: Caudal dysgenesis (sirenomelia) occurs when too little mesoderm forms in the caudal-most region, giving fused lower limbs, vertebral, renal, anorectal and genital defects. It is associated with maternal diabetes, and in mice with mutations in Brachyury (T), WNT and Engrailed. Persistent primitive streak remnants cause sacrococcygeal teratoma instead.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Self-study page (Langman text: caudal dysgenesis); Langman's 15e Ch.5 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: As intraembryonic mesoderm spreads laterally between ectoderm and endoderm, what happens at the margins of the embryonic disc?
options: It replaces the cytotrophoblast of the chorion
It becomes continuous with the extraembryonic mesoderm
It forms the buccopharyngeal and cloacal membranes
It fuses with the decidua basalis of the uterus
questions.explanation: Mesoderm migrates beyond the margin of the disc and merges with the extraembryonic mesoderm (the lecture specifies the splanchnopleuric layer over the yolk sac; Langman mentions both yolk sac and amnion). The buccopharyngeal membrane is precisely where mesoderm does not penetrate.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gastrulation (mesoderm spread) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: The buccopharyngeal (oropharyngeal) membrane consists of ___ and later breaks down to form the ___.
options: ectoderm and endoderm without mesoderm; oral opening
ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm; anal opening
ectoderm and endoderm without mesoderm; anal opening
mesoderm and endoderm only; opening of the trachea
questions.explanation: In the prechordal region, mesoderm does not spread, so ectoderm and endoderm stay in contact as the buccopharyngeal membrane, whose breakdown forms the oral opening. The membrane with the same composition that forms the anal opening is the cloacal membrane.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Buccopharyngeal membrane slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Mesoderm that migrates cranial to the prechordal plate and becomes continuous across the midline forms the:
options: Notochord
Cardiogenic area
Cloacal membrane
Neural plate
questions.explanation: Mesoderm spreading cranial to the prechordal plate and meeting across the midline forms the cardiogenic (heart-forming) area. The notochord grows cranially only as far as the prechordal plate.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Buccopharyngeal membrane / Cardiogenic area slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: The cloacal membrane is located ___, and its breakdown forms the ___.
options: cranial to the prechordal plate; future oral opening
at the primitive node; neurenteric canal
in the connecting stalk; umbilical ring
caudal to the primitive streak; future anal opening
questions.explanation: Behind (caudal to) the primitive streak, mesoderm does not intervene between ectoderm and endoderm, forming the cloacal membrane, whose breakdown forms the anal opening. The oral opening comes from the buccopharyngeal membrane at the cranial end.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Cloacal membrane slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Which group consists ENTIRELY of derivatives of endoderm?
options: Thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, thymus, liver, pancreas
Epidermis, hair, mammary glands, lens and pituitary gland
Heart, kidneys, gonads and smooth muscle of the gut wall
Melanocytes, Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia, adrenal medulla
questions.explanation: Endoderm lines the primitive gut tube and its buds, giving the epithelium of the digestive and respiratory tracts, liver, pancreas, thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, thymus, and the lining of the auditory tube and middle ear. The other groups are surface ectoderm, mesoderm and neural crest derivatives.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Derivatives of Endoderm slide figure/chart; Langman's 15e Ch.5-6

questions.stem: What is the normal fate of the primitive streak?
options: It persists throughout life as the nucleus pulposus of the discs
It forms mesoderm until the 4th week, then regresses and disappears
It folds to form the neural tube and later the spinal cord
It becomes incorporated into the umbilical cord at the umbilicus
questions.explanation: The primitive streak produces mesoderm until the 4th week and then shrinks and disappears by the end of that week, leaving a trilaminar disc. The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the notochord, not of the streak.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Fate of primitive streak slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a large mass at the base of the spine (sacrococcygeal region) that contains hair, teeth and gut-like structures, i.e. tissues from all three germ layers. This tumour - the most common tumour in newborns (about 1 in 37,000 births), more frequent in females and capable of becoming malignant - most likely arises from:
options: Remnants of the notochord
Failure of closure of the caudal neuropore
Neural crest cells
Remnants of the primitive streak
questions.explanation: Sacrococcygeal teratoma arises from persistent remnants of the primitive streak, whose pluripotent cells form tissues of all three germ layers. Notochordal remnants give rise to chordoma, not to a trigerminal teratoma.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Self-study page (Langman text: sacrococcygeal teratoma); Fate of primitive streak slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Prenotochordal cells migrate cranially in the midline from the primitive node to form the notochordal process. How far do they migrate?
options: Up to the cloacal membrane
Into the connecting stalk
Up to the prechordal plate
Beyond the cardiogenic area into the septum transversum
questions.explanation: Prenotochordal cells migrate cranially from the primitive node until they reach the prechordal plate, forming the notochordal process in the median plane. The cloacal membrane lies caudal to the streak, in the opposite direction.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Notochord formation slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: The solid notochordal process becomes the notochordal canal when:
options: Its floor fuses with the overlying surface ectoderm
It acquires a lumen by extension of the primitive pit
Neural crest cells invade and hollow out its core
It detaches completely from the underlying endoderm
questions.explanation: The notochordal process acquires a lumen through extension of the primitive pit, becoming the tubular notochordal canal. Detachment from the endoderm is the final step that forms the definitive notochord.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Notochord formation slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: During notochord formation, the floor of the notochordal canal fuses with the underlying endoderm and the fused layers then degenerate. What is the immediate result?
options: The definitive notochord forms at once as a cord free of the endoderm
The amniotic cavity is obliterated as the canal opens into it
The cloacal membrane ruptures to form the opening of the anal canal
Openings link the canal with the yolk sac, leaving a flat notochordal plate
questions.explanation: Degeneration of the fused floor creates openings between the notochordal canal and the yolk sac and leaves the flattened notochordal plate within the endoderm. Only later does the plate fold and detach from the endoderm to become the definitive notochord.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Notochord formation slide (notochordal plate, definitive notochord); Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Remnants of the notochord persist in the adult as the:
options: Annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral discs
Vertebral bodies
Nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs
Ligamentum flavum
questions.explanation: The notochord degenerates as the vertebral column forms, but its remnants persist as the nucleus pulposus. The annulus fibrosus and vertebral bodies develop from sclerotome.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Fate of notochord slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5 & Ch.10

questions.stem: Which is the most important inductive function of the notochord?
options: Induction of the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate
Induction of the hypoblast to form the primary yolk sac
Induction of the trophoblast to secrete chorionic gonadotropin
Induction of the epiblast to form the primitive streak
questions.explanation: The notochord is the primary inductor of the neural plate, and thus of the neural tube and the future nervous system. The primitive streak forms before the notochord, so the notochord cannot induce it.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Functional significance of notochord slide; Neural tube development slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5-6

questions.stem: All of the following are functions of the notochord EXCEPT:
options: It defines the primordial axis of the embryo
It gives some rigidity to the embryo
It gives rise to the neurons of the spinal cord
It serves as the basis for development of the axial skeleton
questions.explanation: The notochord defines the axis, gives rigidity, serves as the basis for the axial skeleton, indicates the site of the vertebral column and induces the neural tube. Spinal cord neurons come from the neural tube (neuroectoderm), not from the notochord itself.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Functional significance of notochord slide; Langman's 15e Ch.5

questions.stem: Which structure is derived from endoderm?
options: Epidermis of the skin of the back
Smooth muscle of the gut wall
Epithelial lining of the trachea
Lens and outer surface of the cornea
questions.explanation: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract (larynx except epiglottis, trachea, bronchi, alveoli) as well as the gut. Smooth muscle of the gut wall is from splanchnic mesoderm, the classic distractor.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Derivatives of Endoderm slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.5-6 & Ch.14

questions.stem: Which lining is derived from ectoderm rather than endoderm?
options: Lining of the upper part of the anal canal (above the pectinate line)
Lining of the tympanic (middle ear) cavity
Lining of the lower part of the anal canal (below the pectinate line)
Lining of the urinary bladder
questions.explanation: The lower part of the anal canal (with the terminal urethra and external auditory meatus) is lined by ectoderm. The upper anal canal above the pectinate line, the middle ear cavity/auditory tube and the bladder are lined by endoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Derivatives of Ectoderm slide and Derivatives of Endoderm slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.5 & Ch.15

questions.stem: Which group consists ENTIRELY of ectodermal derivatives?
options: Epidermis, dermis and skeletal muscle of the back
Lens, thyroid follicular cells and hepatocytes
Epidermis, mammary glands, lens and pituitary gland
Nervous system, heart muscle and kidneys
questions.explanation: Epidermis and appendages (including mammary glands), lens, outer corneal surface and pituitary gland are all ectodermal. Dermis and skeletal muscle are mesodermal, and thyroid follicular cells and hepatocytes are endodermal.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Derivatives of Ectoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Which sequence of neural tube formation is correct?
options: Hypoblast induces neural plate -> neural groove between neural folds -> folds fuse, closure proceeding only caudally
Notochord induces neural plate -> neural groove between neural folds -> folds fuse, closure proceeding cranially and caudally
Neural folds fuse first -> neural plate forms beneath them -> notochord appears last to support the tube
Paraxial mesoderm folds into a tube -> surface ectoderm covers it -> neural crest fills the central canal
questions.explanation: Induced by the notochord, the overlying ectoderm forms the neural plate, which invaginates as the neural groove between neural folds; the folds fuse into a tube, with closure progressing both cranially and caudally (Langman: starting in the future cervical region). The inducer is the notochord, not the hypoblast.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Neural tube development slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: A fetus is diagnosed with anencephaly, which results from failure of the cranial (anterior) neuropore to close. Normally this neuropore closes at about:
options: Day 18
Day 25
Day 28
Day 35
questions.explanation: The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 28. Failure of cranial closure causes anencephaly, and failure of caudal closure causes spina bifida.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Neural tube development slide (neuropore closure); Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.18

questions.stem: A newborn has a lumbosacral spina bifida with myelomeningocele, a defect associated with failure of the caudal (posterior) neuropore to close. Normally this neuropore closes at about:
options: Day 14
Day 20
Day 25
Day 28
questions.explanation: The caudal neuropore closes at about day 28, after the cranial neuropore (day 25). Its failure leads to defects of the lower spine such as spina bifida, and periconceptional folic acid lowers the risk of such neural tube defects.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Neural tube development slide (neuropore closure); Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.18

questions.stem: Neural crest cells separate from the ectoderm at the angle between the neural folds and the surface ectoderm. Which group consists ENTIRELY of neural crest derivatives?
options: Kidneys, gonads and the genital ducts of both sexes
Lens, epidermis, hair follicles and anterior pituitary
Vertebrae, ribs and the skeletal muscles of the limbs
Facial bones, spinal ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla
questions.explanation: Neural crest derivatives include facial bones (via the pharyngeal arches), sensory (spinal) and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, chromaffin cells of the suprarenal (adrenal) medulla, melanocytes and the leptomeninges. Kidneys, gonads and genital ducts come from intermediate mesoderm, while lens, epidermis, hair and anterior pituitary come from surface ectoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Neural crest cell slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 (Table: neural crest derivatives)

questions.stem: Neural crest cells give rise to all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Melanocytes
Pia mater and arachnoid mater
Conotruncal (outflow-tract) septum of the heart
Skeletal muscles of the limbs
questions.explanation: Limb skeletal muscle comes from the dermomyotome of somites (paraxial mesoderm). Melanocytes, the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid) and the conotruncal septum (the 'heart septa' on the slide) are neural crest derivatives.
questions.source: Lecture: Third Week of Development (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Neural crest cell slide; Lecture: Embryonic Period - Paraxial mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.11

questions.stem: The embryonic period, also called the period of organogenesis, extends from:
options: The 3rd to the 8th week of development
Fertilization to the end of the 2nd week
The 9th week until birth
The 1st to the 12th week
questions.explanation: The embryonic period runs from week 3 to week 8, when the germ layers form the primordia of all major organs. From week 9 until birth is the fetal period.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Embryonic period slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two major events of the embryonic period?
options: Organogenesis is growth of formed organs; morphogenesis is formation of the germ layers
Organogenesis occurs in the fetal period; morphogenesis occurs in the first two weeks
Organogenesis forms the placenta; morphogenesis forms the fetal membranes and cord
Organogenesis forms organ primordia; morphogenesis changes body form to look human
questions.explanation: In organogenesis, stem cells of the three germ layers form organ primordia (CNS, gut and its glands, heart, respiratory and urogenital systems); in morphogenesis, the embryo's shape becomes more human. Growth of organs that are already formed characterizes the fetal period.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Embryonic period and Organogenesis slides; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: A woman takes a known teratogenic drug during weeks 4-7 of pregnancy. Compared with exposure late in pregnancy, exposure at this time is most likely to cause:
options: No effect, because the placenta blocks all drugs during this period
Only mild growth restriction, because the organs are already fully formed
Major structural (morphological) birth defects, because organ primordia are being established
Either death of the conceptus or complete recovery, with no possibility of malformation
questions.explanation: Weeks 3-8 (organogenesis) are the most sensitive period for inducing structural birth defects. The 'all-or-none' response describes exposure in weeks 1-2, before the germ layers form, and the fetal period mainly shows effects on growth and function.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Embryonic period / Organogenesis slides; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.9

questions.stem: From medial to lateral, the intraembryonic mesoderm on each side of the midline differentiates into:
options: Lateral plate mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and intermediate mesoderm
Paraxial mesoderm, intermediate mesoderm and lateral plate mesoderm
Intermediate mesoderm, lateral plate mesoderm and paraxial mesoderm
Somatic mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and splanchnic mesoderm
questions.explanation: Cells near the midline form the thick paraxial mesoderm; the lateral part stays thin as lateral plate mesoderm; and between them lies the longitudinal strip of intermediate mesoderm. Somatic and splanchnic are the two layers of the lateral plate, not separate columns.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Derivatives of intraembryonic mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Paraxial mesoderm becomes segmented into somites. In what sequence do somites appear?
options: Caudo-cranial, beginning in the coccygeal region
Simultaneously along the whole length of the embryo
Cranio-caudal, beginning in the occipital region
Starting in the thoracic region and spreading both ways
questions.explanation: Somites form in a cranio-caudal sequence, beginning in the occipital region at about day 20 and adding roughly three pairs per day (Langman). This is why somite number can be used to estimate age.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Paraxial mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Which list gives the correct number of somite pairs in each region?
options: 4 occipital, 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 coccygeal
2 occipital, 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
4 occipital, 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 8-10 coccygeal
4 occipital, 8 cervical, 10 thoracic, 6 lumbar, 4 sacral, 8-10 coccygeal
questions.explanation: There are 4 occipital, 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 8-10 coccygeal pairs (about 42-44). The trap is '7 cervical': there are 7 cervical vertebrae but 8 cervical somites, matching the 8 cervical spinal nerves.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Paraxial mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Somites first appear at about day 20, and new pairs are added at about three pairs per day. An embryo has 26-29 pairs of somites. Its approximate age is:
options: Day 14
Day 28
Day 42
Day 56
questions.explanation: In Langman's somite-age table, 26-29 somites corresponds to about day 28 (17-20 at day 25, 34-35 at day 30). By day 42 somite formation (42-44 pairs, end of week 5) is complete, so age is then estimated by CRL instead.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - How to determine age: Number of somites slide (28-somite embryo) and Table 6.2 slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.6 (Table 6.2)

questions.stem: The sclerotome of each somite gives rise mainly to the:
options: Skeletal muscles of the back
Dermis of the skin of the back
Vertebrae and ribs
Kidneys and gonads
questions.explanation: The sclerotome forms the vertebrae and ribs, while the dermomyotome forms skeletal muscle and dermis. (The slide also lists the sternum, but per Langman the sternum develops from the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm.)
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Paraxial mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.10

questions.stem: The dermomyotome of a somite gives rise to:
options: Vertebrae, ribs and intervertebral discs
Smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gut
Epidermis, hair follicles and nails
Skeletal muscle and dermis of the skin
questions.explanation: The dermomyotome gives skeletal muscle (myotome) and dermis (dermatome; Langman: dermis of the back). Epidermis and hair follicles are surface ectoderm, and gut smooth muscle is splanchnic mesoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Paraxial mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.11

questions.stem: A stillborn fetus has bilateral renal agenesis together with absent gonads and abnormal genital ducts. A developmental defect of which mesodermal subdivision best explains this combination?
options: Paraxial mesoderm
Somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Intermediate mesoderm
questions.explanation: Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital structures: kidneys, gonads and genital ducts. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, giving the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.16

questions.stem: The lateral plate mesoderm splits into somatic (parietal) and splanchnic (visceral) layers. What separates the two layers?
options: The intraembryonic coelom
The extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity)
The notochord
The amniotic cavity
questions.explanation: Lateral plate mesoderm is divided by the intraembryonic coelom into somatic and splanchnic layers. The extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity) instead splits the extraembryonic mesoderm in week 2.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: The somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm contributes mainly to the:
options: Thoracic and abdominal (body) walls
Heart and smooth muscle of the gut
Kidneys and gonads
Vertebrae and ribs
questions.explanation: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm, together with the overlying ectoderm, forms the lateral and ventral body walls (thoracic and abdominal walls). The heart and gut smooth muscle come from the splanchnic layer.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: The splanchnic (visceral) layer of lateral plate mesoderm gives rise to the:
options: Skeletal muscles of the thoracic and abdominal walls
Dermis of the skin and skeletal muscles of the back
Heart and smooth muscle of the gut and respiratory tract
Epithelial lining of the gut and respiratory tract
questions.explanation: Splanchnic mesoderm, which is applied to the endoderm, forms the heart and the smooth muscle and connective tissue of the gut and respiratory tract. The epithelial lining of the gut is endoderm.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: The intraembryonic coelom gives rise to the:
options: Amniotic, chorionic and yolk sac cavities
Pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities
Chorionic cavity (extraembryonic coelom)
Lumen of the gut tube and its derivatives
questions.explanation: The intraembryonic coelom becomes the three body cavities: pericardial, pleural and peritoneal. The chorionic cavity is the extraembryonic coelom, a different space.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm slide (Note on intraembryonic coelom); Langman's 15e Ch.7

questions.stem: Folding of the embryo occurs in two planes, producing:
options: Dorsal and ventral folds of the amnion
Amniotic and chorionic folds around the disc
One median fold along the primitive streak
Head and tail folds plus two lateral folds
questions.explanation: The flat trilaminar disc folds cephalocaudally (head and tail folds) and laterally (two lateral folds), producing a cylindrical embryo. The lateral folds bring the body walls together ventrally.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Folding of embryo slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: As a result of the head fold, the septum transversum, the primordium of the heart and the oropharyngeal membrane move onto the ventral surface of the embryo. After folding, which of these lies MOST CAUDALLY?
options: Septum transversum
Primordium of the heart
Oropharyngeal membrane
They lie side by side at the same level
questions.explanation: These structures come to lie ventrally in caudal-to-cranial order: septum transversum (most caudal), heart, then oropharyngeal membrane (most cranial). The septum transversum, now caudal to the heart, later contributes the central tendon of the diaphragm.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Results of folding (Head fold) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: Which is a result of the tail (caudal) fold?
options: Heart and septum transversum move to the ventral surface of the embryo
Oropharyngeal membrane moves to the dorsal surface of the head region
Midgut loses its connection with the yolk sac and vitelline duct
Connecting stalk moves to the ventral surface; allantois partly incorporated
questions.explanation: Tail folding shifts the connecting stalk (future umbilical cord) to the ventral surface and partially incorporates the allantois into the embryo. The heart and septum transversum move ventrally with the head fold.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Results of folding (Tail fold) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: Before folding, the primitive streak lies cranial to the cloacal membrane. After the tail fold, the primitive streak (or its remnant) comes to lie:
options: Cranial to the oropharyngeal membrane
Within the connecting stalk at the umbilicus
Dorsal to the neural tube in the cervical region
Caudal to the cloacal membrane
questions.explanation: Tail folding flips the caudal end ventrally, so the primitive streak, originally cranial to the cloacal membrane, ends up caudal to it. This is why streak remnants present as sacrococcygeal masses.
