questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Results of folding (Tail fold) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: After folding, the gut tube is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut. Which part remains connected to the yolk sac, and by what structure?
options: Midgut, via the vitelline duct
Foregut, via the oropharyngeal membrane
Hindgut, via the allantois
Midgut, via the cloacal membrane
questions.explanation: The midgut stays connected to the yolk sac through the vitelline duct. The foregut is closed cranially by the oropharyngeal membrane and the hindgut caudally by the cloacal membrane.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gut tube slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6-7

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with painless rectal bleeding. A scan shows ectopic gastric mucosa in a diverticulum on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. This anomaly is a remnant of the:
options: Allantois
Cloacal membrane
Notochord
Vitelline duct
questions.explanation: A Meckel (ileal) diverticulum is a persistent part of the vitelline (vitello-intestinal) duct, which normally links the midgut to the yolk sac; it may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue that ulcerates and bleeds. A persistent allantois (urachus) affects the bladder and umbilicus instead.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Gut tube slide (midgut-vitelline duct); Langman's 15e Ch.15 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: The pharyngeal arches, which contribute greatly to the characteristic external appearance of the embryo, appear during the:
options: 2nd and 3rd weeks
4th and 5th weeks
8th and 9th weeks
10th to 12th weeks
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal arches appear in the 4th and 5th weeks (the slide figure shows them at 25 days, 28 days and 5 weeks). In weeks 2 and 3 the embryo is still a flat germ disc with no arches.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of pharyngeal arches slide and figure; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.17

questions.stem: Which best describes the external appearance of the embryo during the second month?
options: Human-like, with a large head and forming face, eyes, ears, nose and limbs
A flat trilaminar disc with a primitive streak and notochord
Plump, with abundant subcutaneous fat and lanugo hair covering the body
A bilaminar disc suspended in the chorionic cavity by a connecting stalk
questions.explanation: During the second month, head size increases and the face, eyes, ears, nose and limbs form, so the embryo looks increasingly human (the slide figure shows this at 7 weeks). Subcutaneous fat and lanugo are features of the fetal period.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - External appearance in the second month slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: Limb buds, which later elongate and become divided into three segments, first appear (according to the lecture) in the:
options: 3rd week
5th week
8th week
12th week
questions.explanation: Limb buds appear in the 5th week (Langman: visible at the end of the 4th / beginning of the 5th week, upper limbs slightly ahead of lower). By the 8th week the digits are already well formed.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of upper and lower limbs slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.12

questions.stem: Digital rays appear in the hand and foot plates, after which the fingers and toes separate. By which week are the fingers and toes well formed?
options: 5th week
6th week
8th week
12th week
questions.explanation: The fingers and toes are well formed by the 8th week, the end of the embryonic period. Digital rays first appear earlier (around weeks 6-7), but the digits are not separated then.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of upper and lower limbs slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.12

questions.stem: In the early 1960s, mothers who took the sedative thalidomide in early pregnancy gave birth to infants with severe limb reductions (amelia/meromelia). Based on the timing of limb development, the period of greatest limb sensitivity to this drug was most likely:
options: Week 1, during cleavage in the uterine tube
Weeks 4-6, as the limb buds appear and grow
Week 2, during implantation and bilaminar disc formation
Weeks 20-24, during fetal growth and maturation
questions.explanation: Limb buds appear at about week 5 and grow rapidly over the next weeks; Langman places the thalidomide-sensitive period for limbs at about days 24-36. Weeks 1-2 precede organ formation, and by weeks 20-24 the limbs are already formed.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Formation of upper and lower limbs slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 & Ch.12 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Physiological herniation of the intestinal loops into the umbilical cord begins in the ___ week, and the loops normally return to the abdominal cavity by the ___ week.
options: 3rd; 6th
6th; 12th
8th; 28th
12th; 20th
questions.explanation: Herniation starts in the 6th week, when rapid growth of the gut (and liver) outpaces the small abdominal cavity, and the loops return by the 12th week (end of the 3rd month; Langman notes that return begins in the 10th week).
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Herniation of intestinal loops slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6 & Ch.15

questions.stem: A routine ultrasound at 9 weeks shows loops of bowel within the base of the umbilical cord; the abdominal wall is otherwise intact. The most appropriate interpretation is:
options: Normal physiological herniation, expected to return by about the 12th week
Omphalocele from failure of the intestinal loops to return, requiring surgery
Gastroschisis due to failure of the lateral body wall folds to close
Persistent vitelline duct forming a Meckel diverticulum within the cord
questions.explanation: Herniation of intestinal loops into the umbilical cord is normal from the 6th to the 12th week. Only failure of the loops to return after this period produces an omphalocele, so the finding at 9 weeks is physiological.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Herniation of intestinal loops slide; Langman's 15e Ch.7 & Ch.15 (Clinical Correlates)

questions.stem: Crown-rump length (CRL) is measured from the:
options: Vertex of the skull to the heel of the foot
Tip of the chin to the tip of the coccyx
Vertex of skull to midpoint between apices of buttocks
Forehead to the umbilicus along the midline
questions.explanation: CRL ('sitting height') runs from the vertex of the skull to the midpoint between the apices of the buttocks. Vertex-to-heel is crown-heel length, which is used later in the fetal period.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - How to determine age: Crown-rump length slide; Langman's 15e Ch.6

questions.stem: An ultrasound of an embryo shows a crown-rump length of 10-14 mm. According to Langman's CRL-age table, its approximate age is:
options: 5 weeks
6 weeks
7 weeks
8 weeks
questions.explanation: Langman's Table 6.3: CRL 5-8 mm = 5 weeks, 10-14 mm = 6 weeks, 17-22 mm = 7 weeks, 28-30 mm = 8 weeks. For example, the 9.8 mm embryo in Fig. 6.22 is in the 5th week, with paddle-shaped forelimbs.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - Crown-rump length slide and Table 6.3 / Fig. 6.22 slide figures; Langman's 15e Ch.6 (Table 6.3)

questions.stem: During the 4th week, while somites are still being added, which is the most useful criterion for estimating the age of an embryo?
options: Counting the number of pairs of somites
Measuring the biparietal diameter
Assessing the amount of subcutaneous fat
Measuring foot length
questions.explanation: While somites are forming (until about the end of week 5), age is best estimated from the number of somite pairs; afterwards, CRL is used. Biparietal diameter and foot length are fetal-period measurements.
questions.source: Lecture: Embryonic Period (3-8 weeks) (Dr. K. H. Afroze) - How to determine age (number of somites; CRL) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.6 (Table 6.2)

questions.stem: According to Langman, which sequence correctly gives the approximate volume of amniotic fluid at 10, 20 and 37 weeks of gestation, respectively?
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid increases from about 30 mL at 10 weeks to 450 mL at 20 weeks and 800–1,000 mL at 37 weeks. A term volume of 1,500–2,000 mL would be polyhydramnios, and a volume below 400 mL oligohydramnios.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — The amniotic cavity slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (pp.108–128)

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the amniotic fluid and membrane described in the lecture?
options: Acting as the main route for fetal gas exchange
Supplying most of the fetal nutrition in the third trimester
Helping to dilate the cervical canal during childbirth
Secreting hCG to maintain the corpus luteum
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid is a protective cushion, prevents adherence of the embryo to the amnion and allows fetal movement. During childbirth the amniotic membrane helps dilate the cervical canal. Gas exchange and nutrition are placental functions, and hCG comes from the syncytiotrophoblast.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — The amniotic cavity slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (pp.108–128)

questions.stem: Which statement about amniotic fluid turnover from the beginning of the fifth month is correct?
options: The fetus swallows about 400 mL/day at term (about half the total volume), and the whole volume is replaced about once every 3 days
The fetus swallows about 40 mL/day at term (less than 5% of the total), and the whole volume is replaced about every 3 hours
Fetal urine added to the fluid is rich in metabolic wastes, because the fetal kidneys are the main excretory organ
The fetus swallows about 400 mL/day at term (about half the total volume), and the whole volume is replaced about every 3 hours
questions.explanation: From the fifth month the fetus drinks about 400 mL/day at term, roughly half the total, and the volume is replaced every 3 hours. Fetal urine is added daily but is mostly water, because the placenta acts as the exchange organ for metabolic wastes.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — The amniotic cavity slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (pp.108–128)

questions.stem: Polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios are defined in the lecture as amniotic fluid volumes of approximately:
options: 800–1,000 mL and less than 30 mL, respectively
1,500–2,000 mL and less than 400 mL, respectively
More than 3,000 mL and less than 800 mL, respectively
450 mL and less than 100 mL, respectively
questions.explanation: Langman defines polyhydramnios as an excess of 1,500–2,000 mL and oligohydramnios as a decrease to under 400 mL. 800–1,000 mL is the normal volume at 37 weeks, and 450 mL the normal volume at 20 weeks.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Polyhydramnios and Oligohydramnios slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: amniotic fluid)

questions.stem: Which pair correctly gives the approximate contributions of idiopathic causes and of maternal diabetes to polyhydramnios?
options: Idiopathic 25%; maternal diabetes 35%
Idiopathic 55%; maternal diabetes 15%
Idiopathic 10%; maternal diabetes 50%
Idiopathic 35%; maternal diabetes 25%
questions.explanation: Idiopathic causes account for about 35% and maternal diabetes about 25%. The rest includes CNS malformations (e.g., anencephaly) and GI atresias (e.g., oesophageal) that stop the fetus swallowing. Swapping the two percentages is the usual mistake.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Polyhydramnios slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: amniotic fluid)

questions.stem: A 30-week ultrasound shows a markedly increased amniotic fluid volume. The fetus has no cranial vault and no forebrain (anencephaly). What is the main mechanism of the fluid excess?
options: Inability of the fetus to swallow amniotic fluid
Increased fetal urine output from overactive kidneys
Leakage of fluid following premature rupture of the membranes
Excess secretion of fluid by the placental villi
questions.explanation: CNS malformations such as anencephaly, and GI defects such as oesophageal atresia, cause polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow the fluid; normally it swallows about 400 mL/day at term. PROM causes loss of fluid, not an excess.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Polyhydramnios slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: amniotic fluid)

questions.stem: A 32-week ultrasound shows severely reduced amniotic fluid, and neither fetal kidney can be identified. Which is the most serious consequence expected at birth?
options: Pulmonary hypoplasia from inability to 'breathe' amniotic fluid
Oesophageal atresia, because there was too little fluid to swallow
Macrosomia, because the uterus no longer compresses the fetus
Anencephaly, because uterine compression deformed the head
questions.explanation: Renal agenesis means no fetal urine, so oligohydramnios develops. With no fluid the fetus cannot 'breathe' it into the lungs, which leads to lung hypoplasia, and the fetus is also constricted (Potter sequence). Oesophageal atresia is a cause of polyhydramnios, not a result of oligohydramnios.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Oligohydramnios slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: amniotic fluid)

questions.stem: Premature rupture of the membranes (PROM), meaning rupture of the membranes before uterine contractions begin, occurs in approximately what percentage of pregnancies?
questions.explanation: PROM occurs in about 10% of pregnancies. The 25% figure is maternal diabetes's share of polyhydramnios, and about 5% is the frequency of preeclampsia.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Polyhydramnios slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: amniotic fluid)

questions.stem: By the end of which month has the expanding amniotic cavity obliterated the chorionic cavity?
options: First month
Second month
Third month
Fifth month
questions.explanation: At the end of the second month the amniotic and chorionic cavities both still exist. By the end of the third month the amnion has expanded and obliterated the chorionic cavity.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — The amniotic cavity slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (pp.108–128)

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern of growth during the fetal period?
options: Growth in length is most striking in the last 2 months, whereas weight gain is most striking in months 3–5, when about 50% of full-term weight is added
Length and weight both increase at a constant rate throughout the fetal period, with no phase of particularly striking growth
Length and weight are both most striking in months 3–5, and only about 10% of full-term weight is added in the last 2 months
Growth in length is most striking in months 3–5, whereas weight gain is most striking in the last 2 months, when about 50% of full-term weight is added
questions.explanation: Length increases most strikingly in the third, fourth and fifth months. Weight gain is most striking in the last 2 months, when about half of the full-term weight is added (Langman: the last ~2–2.5 months). The other options reverse or flatten this pattern.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Main events in the fetal period slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: The head makes up approximately what proportion of the CRL at the beginning of the 3rd month, and of the CHL at the beginning of the 5th month and at birth, respectively?
options: One third; one half; one quarter
One half; one third; one quarter
One quarter; one third; one half
One half; one quarter; one eighth
questions.explanation: The head is about half of the CRL at the start of the 3rd month, a third of the CHL at the start of the 5th month, and a quarter of the CHL at birth. Body growth speeds up while head growth slows, so the head's relative size falls steadily; it never increases.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Growth of the head and body slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: According to Langman's Table 8.1, a fetus with a crown–rump length of 15–19 cm and a weight of 250–450 g is at approximately which gestational age?
options: 9–12 weeks
13–16 weeks
17–20 weeks
21–24 weeks
questions.explanation: Table 8.1 gives 17–20 weeks as CRL 15–19 cm and 250–450 g. For comparison: 9–12 wk is 5–8 cm/10–45 g, 13–16 wk 9–14 cm/60–200 g, 21–24 wk 20–23 cm/500–820 g, and 37–38 wk 35–36 cm/3,000–3,400 g. Length grows fast mid-gestation while weight is still low.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — slide figure (Table 8.1, growth in length and weight); Langman's 15e Ch.8, Table 8.1

questions.stem: The crown–rump length (CRL) corresponds to which body measurement, and what is its approximate value at 9–12 weeks (Table 8.1)?
options: Sitting height; 5–8 cm
Standing height; 5–8 cm
Sitting height; 15–19 cm
Standing height; 35–36 cm
questions.explanation: CRL is the 'sitting height'; the crown–heel length (CHL) is the standing height. At 9–12 weeks the CRL is about 5–8 cm (weight 10–45 g). 15–19 cm is the 17–20-week value and 35–36 cm the 37–38-week value.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — slide figure (Table 8.1, growth in length and weight); Langman's 15e Ch.8, Table 8.1

questions.stem: By which week are primary ossification centers present in the long bones, and are the external genitalia developed enough for fetal sex to be determined by ultrasound?
options: 8th week
12th week
20th week
26th week
questions.explanation: By the 12th week, primary ossification centres are present in the long bones and fetal sex can be determined by ultrasound. The 8th week is the end of the embryonic period, and 26–28 weeks is when survival reaches about 90%.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Development by month slides (3rd–7th month, last 2 months); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Lanugo hair covering the body, visible eyebrows and head hair, and the mother first feeling fetal movements (quickening) are characteristic of which month?
options: 3rd month
4th month
5th month
7th month
questions.explanation: During the 5th month the fetus is covered with fine lanugo hair, the eyebrows and head hair become visible, and the mother can feel fetal movements (quickening). Vernix caseosa and well-rounded contours belong to the last 2 months.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Development by month slides (3rd–7th month, last 2 months); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A fetus born early in the sixth month has thin, reddish skin and great difficulty surviving. What is the main reason for its poor chance of survival?
options: Primary ossification centres have not yet appeared in the long bones
Immature respiratory system and CNS, with poor coordination between them
The testes have not yet descended into the scrotum
Vernix caseosa covering the skin blocks cutaneous respiration
questions.explanation: Several organ systems can function in the 6th month, but the respiratory system and CNS are not developed enough and their coordination is not established. The thin reddish skin reflects the lack of subcutaneous fat. Ossification centres have been present since week 12, and vernix appears at term.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Development by month slides (3rd–7th month, last 2 months); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A fetus delivered at 27 weeks is admitted to the NICU. According to Langman, what are its approximate CRL, weight and chance of survival?
options: CRL ~15 cm; weight ~500 g; ~90% chance of survival
CRL ~36 cm; weight ~3,200 g; ~99% chance of survival
CRL ~25 cm; weight ~1,100 g; ~90% chance of survival
CRL ~25 cm; weight ~2,500 g; ~50% chance of survival
questions.explanation: At 26–28 weeks the fetus has a CRL of about 25 cm and weighs about 1,100 g (Table 8.1: 25–28 wk, 24–27 cm, 900–1,300 g). If born then, it has about a 90% chance of survival. CRL 36 cm and about 3,000–3,400 g are term values.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Development by month slides (3rd–7th month, last 2 months); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: During the last 2 months the fetus acquires well-rounded contours, and at full term the skin is covered by a whitish, fatty substance composed of sebaceous gland secretions. This substance is:
options: Vernix caseosa
Lanugo hair
Wharton's jelly
Meconium
questions.explanation: Vernix caseosa is the whitish fatty coating of sebaceous secretions seen at term, and the rounded contours come from deposition of subcutaneous fat. Lanugo is the fine hair of the 5th month, and Wharton's jelly is the connective tissue of the umbilical cord.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Development by month slides (3rd–7th month, last 2 months); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which set of values is typical of a normal newborn at term, according to the lecture?
options: Weight 1,100–2,000 g; CRL ~25 cm; CHL ~36 cm; head circumference 25–28 cm
Weight 2,500–4,000 g; CRL ~36 cm; CHL ~50 cm; head circumference 32–38 cm
Weight 4,000–5,000 g; CRL ~50 cm; CHL ~70 cm; head circumference 40–45 cm
Weight 2,500–4,000 g; CRL ~15 cm; CHL ~30 cm; head circumference 20–24 cm
questions.explanation: At birth, an appropriate-for-gestational-age weight is 2,500–4,000 g (mostly 3,000–3,400 g), CRL about 36 cm, CHL about 50 cm and head circumference 32–38 cm. The skull has the largest circumference of any body part, which matters for passage through the birth canal, and the testes should be in the scrotum.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — At the time of birth slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: According to Langman's developmental horizons (Table 8.2), which pairing of a fetal function with the age at which it first appears is correct?
options: Eyes sensitive to light — 28 weeks
Taste buds appear — 24 weeks
Sucking movements — 10 weeks
Respiratory movements — 7 weeks
questions.explanation: Table 8.2: taste buds appear at 7 weeks, swallowing at 10 weeks, respiratory movements at 14–16 weeks, sucking movements at 24 weeks, some sounds can be heard at 24–26 weeks, and the eyes become sensitive to light at 28 weeks. Each distractor attaches a function to another function's age.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — slide figure (Table 8.2, developmental horizons); Langman's 15e Ch.8, Table 8.2

questions.stem: An obstetrician dates pregnancy from the onset of the last normal menstrual period (LNMP), whereas an embryologist dates it from fertilization. The expected date of birth is therefore:
options: 266 days (38 weeks) after the LNMP, or 280 days (40 weeks) after fertilization
280 days (40 weeks) after both the LNMP and fertilization
300 days (43 weeks) after the LNMP, or 266 days (38 weeks) after fertilization
280 days (40 weeks) after the LNMP, or 266 days (38 weeks) after fertilization
questions.explanation: Birth is expected about 280 days (40 weeks) after the onset of the LNMP, or more accurately 266 days (38 weeks) after fertilization, which happens about 2 weeks after the LNMP. Reversing the two values is the classic error.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Length of pregnancy slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Time of birth)

questions.stem: Which definition relating to the length of pregnancy is correct according to the lecture?
options: Late preterm — 30 to less than 34 weeks
Post-term — after 40 weeks
Preterm — less than 34 weeks
Full term — 37 to 42 weeks
questions.explanation: Full term is 37–42 weeks. Preterm is less than 37 weeks, late preterm is 34 to less than 37 weeks, and post-term is after 42 weeks. Each distractor shifts one of these cut-offs.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Length of pregnancy slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Time of birth)

questions.stem: A woman with uncertain dates has an ultrasound at 22 weeks to estimate gestational age. Which measurements are most appropriate at this stage?
options: Crown–rump length alone, as used in the first trimester
Biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference and femur length
Amniotic fluid volume and placental thickness alone
Head-to-CHL ratio and the number of placental cotyledons
questions.explanation: Ultrasound measures CRL accurately in weeks 7–14. In weeks 16–30 the measurements used are biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference and femur length. Ultrasound can also detect birth defects, and fetal size matters especially when the mother has a small pelvis.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Role of ultrasound slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A baby born at 40 weeks weighs 2,350 g, which is below the 10th percentile for gestational age. Which description is correct?
options: Both low birth weight (LBW) and small for gestational age (SGA)
SGA but not LBW, because LBW applies only to preterm infants
LBW but not SGA, because SGA applies only to preterm infants
Appropriate for gestational age, because term infants cannot be LBW
questions.explanation: LBW means a weight under 2,500 g regardless of gestational age, so term babies can be LBW. SGA means a weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age, and an SGA baby may be pathologically small (IUGR) or constitutionally small (normal). This baby meets both definitions.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Low birth weight / SGA slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: low birth weight)

questions.stem: IUGR may be symmetrical or asymmetrical. In asymmetrical IUGR, which part of the fetus is characteristically relatively spared?
options: The head
The abdomen
The limbs
No part; all growth parameters are reduced proportionally
questions.explanation: In asymmetrical IUGR the head (brain) is relatively spared while body and abdominal growth lag, so the head looks large for the body. In symmetrical IUGR all parameters are reduced in proportion.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — IUGR slide and slide figure (symmetrical vs asymmetrical IUGR); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which statement about intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is correct?
options: About 1 in 200 babies have IUGR, and they are at increased risk of neonatal hypoglycemia
About 1 in 10 babies have IUGR, and they are at increased risk of neonatal hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia
About 1 in 10 babies have IUGR, and they are at increased risk of neonatal hypercalcemia and macrosomia
About 1 in 2 babies have IUGR, with no increase in neonatal morbidity
questions.explanation: About 1 in 10 babies have IUGR. They are at risk of neurological problems, congenital malformations, meconium aspiration, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and RDS. Causes include chromosomal and genetic defects, teratogens, congenital infections, poor maternal health and nutrition, smoking and alcohol, placental insufficiency and multiple births. 1 in 200 is the frequency of a single umbilical artery.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — IUGR slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: low birth weight)

questions.stem: 'What happens in the womb does not stay in the womb.' Adults who had IUGR have a greater chance of developing which of the following later in life?
options: Laron dwarfism with marked short stature and blue sclera
Congenital rubella syndrome with cataracts and deafness
Skeletal dysplasia caused by an FGFR3 gene mutation
Metabolic syndrome (e.g., obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes)
questions.explanation: Babies with IUGR have a greater chance as adults of developing metabolic syndrome: obesity, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Laron dwarfism and FGFR3 skeletal dysplasia are genetic conditions, not consequences of growth restriction.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — IUGR slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Clinical Correlates: low birth weight)

questions.stem: The major growth-promoting factor during fetal life is:
options: Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)
Growth hormone (GH)
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Relaxin
questions.explanation: Fetal tissues express IGF-1, serum levels correlate with fetal growth, and IGF-1 gene mutations cause IUGR that continues after birth. GH and its receptor control postnatal growth and play no role in fetal growth.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — IUGR (IGF-1) and Dwarfism slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has marked short stature and blue sclerae. His birth weight was normal. Serum GH is high, and genetic testing shows a mutation in the growth hormone receptor (GHR) gene. Which statement best explains his condition?
options: IGF-1 gene mutation; growth retardation began in utero and continued after birth
Laron dwarfism; IUGR is always present because GH is the main fetal growth factor
Laron dwarfism; there was no IUGR because GH has no role in fetal growth
Constitutional SGA; catch-up growth is expected at puberty
questions.explanation: A GHR mutation causes Laron dwarfism, with marked postnatal short stature and blue sclera but normal size at birth, because GH has no role in fetal development (fetal growth is IGF-1-driven). An IGF-1 gene mutation, by contrast, causes IUGR that continues after birth.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — IUGR (IGF-1) and Dwarfism slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Newborn twins are shown side by side: one is small for gestational age (SGA) and the other appropriate for gestational age (AGA). The placenta was monochorionic. What is the most probable explanation of their size discrepancy?
options: Laron dwarfism (GHR mutation) in the smaller twin
Feto-fetal transfusion via shared placental anastomoses
Maternal diabetes affecting only the larger twin
Different gestational ages of the two twins
questions.explanation: Twins sharing a monochorionic placenta can have unbalanced vascular anastomoses. In feto-fetal transfusion the donor twin becomes growth-restricted with oligohydramnios, while the recipient is larger, which explains the SGA/AGA pair. Laron dwarfism does not cause prenatal growth restriction, and twins have the same gestational age.
questions.source: Lecture: Fetal Period (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — LBW slide figure (newborn twins, SGA vs AGA); Lecture: Twinning (FFTS); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which description fits a normal full-term placenta?
options: Discoid; 30–35 cm in diameter; about 1 cm thick; about 1,000 g
Oval; about 10 cm in diameter; about 3 cm thick; about 250 g
Discoid; 15–25 cm in diameter; about 6 cm thick; about 1,500 g
Discoid; 15–25 cm in diameter; about 3 cm thick; 500–600 g
questions.explanation: At term the placenta is discoid, 15–25 cm in diameter, about 3 cm thick and weighs 500–600 g. Each distractor changes one or more of these values.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Gross anatomy slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which feature characterizes the fetal surface of the placenta?
options: Irregular, with 15–20 cotyledons separated by deep grooves made by septa
Covered by decidua basalis and receiving the spiral arteries
Formed by the chorion laeve and devoid of blood vessels
Smooth, covered by amnion, with chorionic vessels converging on the cord
questions.explanation: The fetal surface is smooth and covered by amnion, with chorionic vessels converging on the umbilical cord, which is usually attached eccentrically. The irregular surface with 15–20 cotyledons and grooves is the maternal surface.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Fetal surface slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: The maternal surface of a term placenta is irregular and divided by deep grooves, made by the placental septa, into approximately how many cotyledons?
questions.explanation: The maternal surface has 15–20 cotyledons, separated by grooves formed by the placental (decidual) septa. 80–100 is the number of spiral arteries that supply the intervillous spaces.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Maternal surface slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: The fetal and maternal components of the placenta are formed, respectively, by the:
options: Chorion laeve and decidua capsularis
Chorion frondosum and decidua parietalis
Amnion and decidua basalis
Chorion frondosum and decidua basalis
questions.explanation: The fetal part is the chorion frondosum, the villous chorion facing the decidua basalis, and the maternal part is the decidua basalis. The chorion laeve and the decidua capsularis and parietalis do not form the placenta.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Structure of the placenta slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Chorionic villi of the chorion frondosum that penetrate through the decidua basalis and attach the placenta to it are called:
options: Free (nourishing) villi
Primary villi
Secondary villi
Anchoring (fixing) villi
questions.explanation: Anchoring (fixing) villi penetrate the decidua basalis and hold the placenta in place. Free (nourishing) villi float in the intervillous space without penetrating it and are the main exchange surface. Primary and secondary villi are developmental stages, not functional types.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Fetal part slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Maternal blood in one intervillous space can flow freely into neighbouring spaces. Which structural feature explains this?
options: The cotyledons are separated by complete fibrous walls lined by fetal endothelium
Each cotyledon is supplied by one of the two umbilical arteries
The placental (decidual) septa are incomplete, so the cotyledons are only partially separated
The chorionic plate is perforated by the umbilical vein
questions.explanation: Placental septa are incomplete decidual septa that project into the intervillous spaces but do not reach the chorionic plate. The cotyledons are therefore only partially separated (Fig. 8.13) and the intervillous spaces communicate. The umbilical vessels are fetal and never open into the intervillous space.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Maternal part slide and slide figure (Fig. 8.13); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: In the mature placenta, the intervillous spaces, which contain maternal blood, are lined by:
options: Fetal capillary endothelium
Amnion
Cytotrophoblast
Syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: Fig. 8.13 shows the intervillous spaces lined by syncytium (syncytiotrophoblast), so maternal blood is in direct contact with trophoblast. Fetal endothelium lines the fetal capillaries inside the villi, and the amnion covers the fetal surface.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — slide figure (Fig. 8.13, mature placenta); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: In the mature placenta, the intervillous spaces receive maternal blood from approximately how many spiral arteries, and contain about what volume of blood?
options: 80–100 spiral arteries; about 150 mL
15–20 spiral arteries; about 150 mL
80–100 spiral arteries; about 500 mL
2 spiral arteries; about 50 mL
questions.explanation: Chorionic villi erode about 80–100 spiral arteries, and the intervillous spaces of the mature placenta hold about 150 mL of maternal blood. 15–20 is the number of cotyledons, and 500–600 g is the placental weight.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Maternal part / intervillous space slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: The brush border of microvilli on the nourishing villi increases the total exchange surface area of the placenta to approximately:
questions.explanation: The villi, enlarged by the microvillous brush border of the syncytium, provide about 4–14 m² of surface. This greatly increases the rate of exchange between the maternal and fetal circulations.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Nourishing villi (brush border) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: As pregnancy advances, the placenta increases in size and in thickness. These increases are due, respectively, to:
options: Formation of new villi, and extensive arborization (branching) of the villi
Accumulation of amniotic fluid, and thickening of the amnion
Fibrinoid deposition in the intervillous space, and growth of the decidua parietalis
Fusion of the chorion laeve with the placenta, and thickening of the decidua capsularis
questions.explanation: The placenta grows in size as new villi form, and in thickness through extensive arborization of the villi. The amnion, chorion laeve and decidua capsularis/parietalis do not contribute to placental growth.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental growth slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the maternal side of the placental circulation?
options: Oxygenated blood enters the intervillous spaces from the umbilical arteries and drains back towards the fetus through the umbilical vein
Blood enters the intervillous spaces from the endometrial veins at low pressure and leaves them through the spiral arteries at high pressure
Oxygenated blood enters the intervillous spaces from the spiral arteries at higher pressure and drains into the endometrial veins at lower pressure
Maternal blood flows within the fetal capillaries of the chorionic villi, where it mixes freely with the fetal blood
questions.explanation: Maternal arterial blood from the spiral arteries enters the intervillous spaces under higher pressure, bathes the villi, and returns mostly through the lower-pressure endometrial veins, carrying fetal CO2 and wastes. Maternal and fetal blood do not normally mix, and the umbilical vessels are fetal.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental circulation (maternal part) slide and slide figure (Fig. 8.13); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Oxygen and nutrients reach the fetus from the placenta through the:
options: Two umbilical arteries
Spiral arteries
Umbilical vein
Vitelline duct
questions.explanation: Oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood reaches the fetus in the single umbilical vein. The two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood, CO2 and wastes to the placenta, and the spiral arteries are maternal vessels.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental circulation (fetal part) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: In early pregnancy (tertiary villi), the placental barrier separating maternal from fetal blood consists of:
options: Fetal capillary endothelium and syncytiotrophoblast only, with no other intervening layer
Fetal capillary endothelium, fibrinoid material around the vessels, and syncytiotrophoblast
Amnion, chorionic plate, decidua basalis and fetal capillary endothelium
Fetal capillary endothelium, villous mesoderm (connective tissue), cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: The early barrier has four layers: fetal endothelium, villous-core mesoderm (connective tissue), cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. Later it thins to endothelium plus syncytium, and per the lecture fibrinoid surrounds the fetal vessels at term.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental barrier (early pregnancy) slide and slide figure (Fig. 8.8); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: From the 4th month onward (and characteristically by mid-pregnancy, ~20 weeks), the placental barrier in many small villi becomes much thinner. In these villi it then consists of:
options: Fetal capillary endothelium and syncytiotrophoblast
Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Fetal capillary endothelium and cytotrophoblast
Villous mesoderm and syncytiotrophoblast
questions.explanation: As the cytotrophoblast and connective tissue disappear from the exchange areas, fetal endothelium lies directly against the syncytium. This leaves a two-layer barrier that greatly increases the rate of exchange.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental barrier (middle of pregnancy) slide and slide figure (Fig. 8.8); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: According to the lecture, fibrinoid material surrounding the fetal blood vessels forms part of the placental barrier at which stage?
options: Before tertiary villi form
Early pregnancy (tertiary villi)
Middle of pregnancy (~20 weeks)
End of pregnancy
questions.explanation: Per the lecture, the barrier at the end of pregnancy is fetal endothelium, fibrinoid material around the fetal vessels, and syncytiotrophoblast. Early pregnancy has four layers including cytotrophoblast, and mid-pregnancy has only endothelium and syncytium.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placental barrier (end of pregnancy) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which statement about placental functions is correct?
options: Maternal antibodies cannot cross the placenta, so the newborn has no passive immunity
Amino acids, fatty acids and vitamins cannot cross the placenta, so the fetus depends on amniotic fluid for nutrition
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged across the placental membrane by simple diffusion
The placenta has no excretory role; fetal wastes are removed mainly by the fetal kidneys
questions.explanation: The respiratory gases cross by simple diffusion. The placenta also passes electrolytes and nutrients (amino acids, fatty acids, carbohydrates, vitamins), replaces the kidneys in excreting wastes, and transmits maternal antibodies that give passive immunity. Each distractor denies one of these functions.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Functions of placenta slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: During the first 2 months of pregnancy, the syncytiotrophoblast secretes which hormone?
options: Growth hormone (GH)
Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)
Oxytocin
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
questions.explanation: In the first 2 months the syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum. By the end of the 4th month the placenta also produces progesterone, estrogen (estriol), somatomammotropin and relaxin.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Hormone production slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which hormone, secreted by the placenta by the end of the 4th month, softens the ligaments of the pelvis?
options: Relaxin
Somatomammotropin
Human chorionic gonadotropin
Estriol
questions.explanation: Relaxin softens the pelvic ligaments. By the end of the 4th month the placenta also secretes progesterone, estrogen (estriol) and somatomammotropin. hCG is the characteristic hormone of the first 2 months.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Hormone production slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which pairing of a placental anomaly with its category in the lecture's classification is correct?
options: Succenturiate (accessory) placenta — anomaly of shape
Membranous (diffuse) placenta — anomaly of thickness
Fenestrated placenta — anomaly of number
Velamentous placenta — anomaly of site
questions.explanation: The membranous (diffuse) placenta is the anomaly of thickness. Succenturiate (accessory) placenta is an anomaly of number, with double and triple placentas. Fenestrated (central defect), bilobed, trilobed and circumvallate are anomalies of shape. Velamentous and battledore placentas are anomalies of cord attachment, while previa is the anomaly of site.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Congenital anomalies (classification) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks has vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment, completely covering the internal os. What is the diagnosis, and how should she be delivered?
options: Placenta previa lateralis; spontaneous vaginal delivery
Placenta accreta; induction of labour at term
Placenta previa centralis; delivery by Cesarean section
Velamentous placenta; vaginal delivery after induction
questions.explanation: A placenta attached to the lower uterine segment is placenta previa, and complete coverage of the internal os is placenta previa centralis. It can cause severe antepartum haemorrhage, so delivery is by Cesarean section. Placenta previa lateralis lies in the lower segment away from the internal os.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Anomalies according to site (placenta previa) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which pairing of a placental abnormality with its typical haemorrhagic complication is correct?
options: Placenta previa — postpartum haemorrhage only; placenta accreta — antepartum haemorrhage only
Placenta previa — antepartum haemorrhage; placenta accreta/increta/percreta — postpartum haemorrhage
Circumvallate placenta — failure of placental separation; placenta previa — no bleeding risk
Battledore placenta — failure of placental separation; placenta percreta — no bleeding risk
questions.explanation: A previa lies over the lower segment and internal os and can bleed severely before delivery (antepartum). In the accreta spectrum the villi penetrate beyond the endometrium, so the placenta fails to separate after birth, causing severe postpartum haemorrhage.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Placenta previa and degree of penetration slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A placenta has a thick ring of membranes (a double fold of chorion and amnion) on its fetal surface, and its chorionic plate is smaller than its decidual (basal) plate. This is a:
options: Fenestrated placenta
Circumvallate placenta
Membranous placenta
Battledore placenta
questions.explanation: A circumvallate placenta has a thick ring of folded chorion and amnion on the fetal surface, because the chorionic plate is smaller than the decidual plate. A fenestrated placenta has a central defect, and a membranous placenta is abnormally thin.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Anomalies according to shape slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: After delivery the placenta fails to separate, and severe postpartum haemorrhage needs a hysterectomy. Pathology shows chorionic villi passing through the full thickness of the myometrium to the perimetrium, and invading the bladder wall. The diagnosis is:
options: Placenta increta
Placenta accreta
Placenta percreta
Placenta previa marginalis
questions.explanation: In placenta percreta the villi penetrate the whole myometrium to the perimetrium (completely through the wall) and may invade the bladder; it is the deepest form. Increta extends into the uterine muscle but not through it, and accreta is the least deep. All three can prevent placental separation and cause severe postpartum haemorrhage.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Degree of penetration slides and slide figure (placenta accreta spectrum); Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a battledore placenta from a velamentous placenta?
options: Battledore: cord inserted into the membranes; velamentous: cord at the placental margin
Battledore: cord attached centrally; velamentous: cord attached eccentrically
Battledore: cord at the placental margin; velamentous: cord inserted into the membranes
Battledore: central placental defect; velamentous: thick ring of membranes
questions.explanation: In a battledore (marginal) placenta the cord attaches at the margin, resembling a badminton racquet. In a velamentous placenta the cord does not reach the placenta but attaches to the amniotic membrane, and the umbilical vessels run in the membranes. Normal attachment is eccentric on the fetal surface.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Anomalies according to attachment of umbilical cord slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Preeclampsia (maternal hypertension in pregnancy) occurs in approximately what percentage of pregnancies?
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia affects about 5% of pregnancies. It may progress to eclampsia (seizures) and can cause IUGR, fetal death or maternal death, but it is completely reversible by delivery of the baby.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Preeclampsia slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida with obesity, carrying twins, develops hypertension at 34 weeks. Which statement about her condition is correct?
options: First pregnancy and multiple gestation are protective against this condition
It may progress to eclampsia (seizures) and resolves completely after delivery
Eclampsia is defined by the onset of IUGR rather than by maternal seizures
The hypertension typically persists for life despite delivery of the baby
questions.explanation: This is preeclampsia. Risk factors include first pregnancy, obesity, multiple gestation, previous or family history of preeclampsia, hypertension and diabetes. It can progress to eclampsia, defined by seizures, and it is completely reversible by delivery.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Preeclampsia slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: According to the lecture, the normal umbilical cord at birth is approximately:
options: 30–80 cm long (average 50 cm) and 2 cm in diameter
10–20 cm long (average 15 cm) and 0.5 cm in diameter
100–150 cm long (average 120 cm) and 5 cm in diameter
30–80 cm long (average 50 cm) and 6 cm in diameter
questions.explanation: The lecture gives the cord as 30–80 cm long (average 50 cm) and 2 cm in diameter. It is spirally twisted, producing false knots, and covered by amnion. (Langman quotes 50–60 cm.)
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Umbilical cord (characteristics at birth) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which structures are found in the normal umbilical cord at birth?
options: Two arteries and one vein in Wharton's jelly, plus allantoic and vitelline remnants
One umbilical artery and two umbilical veins embedded in Wharton's jelly
Two umbilical arteries and two umbilical veins, with the vitelline vessels
One umbilical artery and one umbilical vein surrounded by decidua basalis
questions.explanation: The primitive cord forms from the connecting stalk (carrying the allantois and umbilical vessels) and the vitelline duct, covered by amnion. At birth it contains Wharton's jelly, 2 umbilical arteries, 1 umbilical vein, and remnants of the allantois (urachus) and vitelline duct.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Umbilical cord (development and contents) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Examining the cut umbilical cord of a newborn, the midwife sees only two vessels: one artery and one vein. Which statement is correct?
options: This occurs in about 1 in 10 newborns and has no clinical significance
This occurs in about 1 in 200 newborns, and essentially all such babies have major cardiac defects
This occurs in about 1 in 200 newborns, and about 20% of such babies have cardiac, renal or other vascular defects
This is the normal arrangement; the cord normally has one artery and one vein
questions.explanation: A single umbilical artery occurs in about 1 in 200 newborns, and about 20% of these babies have cardiac, renal and other vascular defects, so they need further assessment. The normal cord has two arteries and one vein.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Umbilical cord (congenital anomalies) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which pairing of an umbilical cord feature with its consequence is correct?
options: Short cord — abruptio placentae
Long cord — abruptio placentae
Normal spiral twisting — true knots
Short cord — cord looped around the fetal neck
questions.explanation: A short cord can pull the placenta away from its attachment (abruptio placentae). A long cord predisposes to true knots and loops around the neck. Normal spiral twisting produces false knots, not true ones.
questions.source: Lecture: Placenta (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Umbilical cord (characteristics and congenital anomalies) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8

questions.stem: Which statement about birth defects is correct?
options: Birth defects include only structural disorders; behavioral, functional and metabolic disorders present at birth are excluded
'Birth defect', 'congenital malformation' and 'congenital anomaly' are synonymous terms, and the study of these disorders is called teratology (dysmorphology)
The frequency of birth defects differs markedly between Asian, African American, Latin American, White and Native American populations
Teratologists (dysmorphologists) are usually based within departments of obstetric surgery rather than in clinical genetics departments
questions.explanation: These three terms are synonyms covering structural, behavioral, functional and metabolic disorders present at birth, and their study is teratology (Greek teratos, monster) or dysmorphology. Teratologists usually work in clinical genetics departments, and birth defects are nondiscriminatory: frequencies are the same across ethnic groups.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Terminology slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: What are the approximate contributions of genetic factors, environmental factors and gene–environment interaction (multifactorial) to the causes of birth defects?
options: Genetic 55%; environmental 30%; interaction 15%
Genetic 15%; environmental 55%; interaction 30%
Genetic 30%; environmental 15%; interaction 55%
Genetic 30%; environmental 55%; interaction 15%
questions.explanation: Genetic factors account for about 30%, environmental factors about 15%, and the interaction of the environment with genetic susceptibility (multifactorial) the majority, about 55%. For most defects in that last group the specific cause is unknown.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Causes slide and slide figure (causes pie chart); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Major structural anomalies occur in approximately __ of liveborn infants, minor anomalies in __ of newborns, and birth defects account for about __ of infant deaths. Which set completes the statement?
questions.explanation: Major structural anomalies occur in about 3% of liveborn infants and minor anomalies in about 15% of newborns. Birth defects are a leading cause of infant mortality, about 25% of infant deaths. 55% is the share of causes due to gene–environment interaction.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Frequency slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Infants with one, two, and three or more minor anomalies have, respectively, approximately what chance of also having a major malformation?
questions.explanation: The risk of a major malformation is about 3% with one minor anomaly, 10% with two, and 20% with three or more. Minor anomalies such as microtia (graded 1–4 in the slide figure) are indicators that should prompt a search for major defects.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Minor anomalies slide and slide figure (microtia); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A fetus is diagnosed with the second most common autosomal trisomy. About 80% of affected infants are female, and most affected conceptuses die before birth. Which syndrome is this?
options: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)
Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 microdeletion)
questions.explanation: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is the second most common trisomy after Down syndrome. About 80% of affected infants are female, and most die before birth. DiGeorge syndrome is a microdeletion, not a trisomy.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — slide figure (chromosomal abnormalities: Edwards syndrome); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A ventricular septal defect arising from abnormal formation of the heart during the embryonic period is best classified as a:
options: Disruption
Deformation
Malformation
Association
questions.explanation: Malformations occur while structures and organs are forming (embryonic period). They are primary or intrinsic and may mean complete or partial absence of a structure; examples are VSD, ASD, cleft lip/palate and neural tube defects. Disruptions alter structures that have already formed.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Malformations slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A newborn has transverse amputation of several fingers with constriction rings, caused by amniotic bands. This defect is best classified as a:
options: Malformation
Disruption
Deformation
Dysplasia
questions.explanation: Disruptions are secondary (extrinsic) changes to already formed structures caused by destructive processes, mostly environmental. Amniotic band amputations of fingers and transverse limb defects are the classic examples. Malformations are primary errors in formation.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Disruptions slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A baby born after a pregnancy complicated by oligohydramnios has talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) and congenital dislocation of the hip. Both structures were normally formed but were moulded by compression in the amniotic cavity, and the clubfoot corrects with postnatal splinting. These defects are best classified as:
options: Malformations
Disruptions
Dysplasias
Deformations
questions.explanation: Deformations come from mechanical forces acting on an otherwise normal part. They often involve the musculoskeletal system and may be reversible after birth; congenital hip dislocation and talipes equinovarus from compression in oligohydramnios are the examples given. Disruptions, by contrast, destroy tissue (e.g., amniotic bands).
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Deformations slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A child has a generalized skeletal disorder caused by a mutant FGFR3 gene, with abnormal organization of cells into tissue that affects bones throughout the body. This is best described as a:
options: Deformation
Disruption
Association
Dysplasia
questions.explanation: A dysplasia is abnormal organization of specific cells into a tissue, so its effects appear wherever that tissue is present. FGFR3 skeletal dysplasia and ectodermal dysplasia are examples. Dysplasias are mostly due to a single gene defect and have a high recurrence rate.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Dysplasia slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which term describes a group of anomalies occurring together that have a specific common cause, so that a diagnosis is made and the risk of recurrence is known?
options: Association
Syndrome
Sequence
Dysplasia
questions.explanation: A syndrome is a group of anomalies with a specific common cause, so the recurrence risk is known. Examples are Down syndrome (chromosomal) and Van der Woude syndrome (single gene, IRF6). In an association the cause has not been determined.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Syndrome slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A newborn has oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula, imperforate anus, a ventricular septal defect and a radial limb anomaly. No single cause is identified. Which term best describes this pattern, and why is recognizing it important?
options: VACTERL association; finding one component should prompt a search for the others
VACTERL syndrome; the cause and the recurrence risk are known
Potter sequence; a single primary factor triggered a cascade of events
VACTERL deformation; the defects were caused by uterine compression
questions.explanation: VACTERL (vertebral, anal atresia, cardiovascular, tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia, renal/radial, limb) is an association: a non-random clustering of anomalies whose cause has not been determined. Recognizing one or more components should prompt a search for the others. It is not a syndrome, because no specific cause or recurrence risk is known.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Association slide and slide figure (VACTERL); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A stillborn infant had bilateral renal agenesis with severe oligohydramnios, a flattened face, talipes equinovarus, hip dislocation and lung hypoplasia, and died of respiratory failure. This pattern, in which one primary factor sets off a cascade of events, is best termed a:
options: Sequence
Syndrome
Association
Dysplasia
questions.explanation: In a sequence, a single primary factor causes a cascade of events. In Potter sequence, oligohydramnios from defective fetal urine output or chronic leakage leads to fetal compression (flattened face, clubfoot, hip dislocation), lung hypoplasia and death from respiratory failure. An association has no single identified initiating factor.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Sequence slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which microdeletion syndrome results from a deletion at chromosome 22q11?
options: Cri-du-chat syndrome
DiGeorge syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Down syndrome
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11 microdeletion. Cri-du-chat results from a 5p deletion, and Prader-Willi and Angelman are other microdeletion syndromes. Down syndrome is a numerical abnormality (trisomy 21).
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chromosomal abnormalities (microdeletion syndromes) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which gene–condition pairing is correct?
options: Apert syndrome — FGFR3 mutation
Van der Woude syndrome — BRACHYURY mutation
Dicephalus — over-expression of the GOOSECOID gene
Skeletal dysplasia — IRF6 mutation
questions.explanation: Over-expression of GOOSECOID causes dicephalus. Apert syndrome is due to FGFR2, Van der Woude syndrome to IRF6, and skeletal dysplasia to mutant FGFR3. BRACHYURY is the gene linked to caudal dysgenesis in maternal diabetes.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Single-gene defect and Gene over-expression slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: The majority of congenital malformations due to genetic causes follow which pattern of inheritance?
options: Multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance
Single-gene autosomal dominant inheritance
Numerical chromosomal abnormality (aneuploidy)
Microdeletion of a chromosomal region
questions.explanation: Multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance involving many loci accounts for most malformations with a genetic cause. Single-gene defects and chromosomal abnormalities are important but less common.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Multifactorial inheritance slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Cleft lip/palate may occur as an isolated defect, as part of a single-gene syndrome, or with a chromosomal abnormality. The concept that one specific malformation can have many different causes is called:
options: Genetic heterogeneity
Multifactorial inheritance
Gene over-expression
Association
questions.explanation: Genetic heterogeneity means a specific malformation can have many different causes: chromosomal, syndromic or isolated. Holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate and neural tube defects are examples. Multifactorial inheritance instead describes many loci acting together to produce one defect.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Genetic heterogeneity slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Until the early 1940s, congenital malformations were assumed to be primarily hereditary. Which two discoveries established that environmental agents can cause birth defects?
options: Discovery of trisomy 21 and of FGFR3 mutations
Descriptions of Potter sequence and the VACTERL association
Identification of GOOSECOID and BRACHYURY gene functions
Gregg's rubella observations and the thalidomide tragedy
questions.explanation: Sir Norman Gregg, an ophthalmologist, showed that maternal rubella in early pregnancy causes embryonic abnormalities, and the sedative thalidomide showed that drugs cross the placenta and produce birth defects. Many teratogens have been identified since. The distractors are genetic or descriptive findings, not environmental ones.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Environmental factors slide and slide figure (N. Gregg); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which statement concerning the principles of teratology is correct?
options: Exposure after the 8th week is completely safe, because organogenesis is complete
The effect of a teratogen is independent of its dose and the duration of exposure
Teratogenic effects are limited to structural malformations; death, IUGR and functional disorders are not teratogenic outcomes
The most sensitive period for inducing birth defects is the 3rd to 8th weeks (embryonic period), but no stage of development is completely safe
questions.explanation: Weeks 3–8 are the most sensitive period, but no stage is completely safe. Teratogenic effects depend on fetal (and maternal) genotype, dose and duration, and specific mechanisms. Outcomes include death, malformation, IUGR and functional disorders.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Principles of teratology slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus seeks preconception counselling. Which statement is correct?
options: Risk is 3–4 times higher; strict glucose control from before conception reduces it
Risk is 3–4 times higher, but glucose control has no effect on malformation risk
Diabetes increases only the risk of a large baby, not of structural malformations
Glucose control need only start in the third trimester, when malformation risk peaks
questions.explanation: Maternal diabetes raises the risk of congenital anomalies (e.g., neural tube and heart defects, caudal dysgenesis) to 3–4 times that of nondiabetic mothers. Strict glucose control starting before conception and continuing through gestation reduces malformations, because organogenesis happens in weeks 3–8.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Maternal disease (diabetes mellitus) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A newborn has bilateral cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus and hearing loss. The mother, who was not vaccinated, had a febrile rash in the first trimester. The most likely cause is:
options: Cytomegalovirus
Toxoplasma gondii
Rubella virus
Herpes simplex virus
questions.explanation: The classical triad of congenital rubella is cataract, cardiac abnormalities (e.g., PDA) and deafness. Glaucoma, microcephaly and tooth abnormalities may also occur, and vaccination has nearly eliminated the disease. Toxoplasmosis is characterized instead by cerebral calcifications and hydrocephalus.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Infectious agents (rubella) slide and slide figure (classical triad); Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which virus is described as a serious threat because the mother often has no symptoms, while the infant may be severely affected at birth (e.g., microcephaly) or appear normal at birth and later develop hearing loss, visual impairment and intellectual disability?
options: Rubella virus
Herpes simplex virus
Varicella-zoster virus
Cytomegalovirus
questions.explanation: CMV is a serious threat because maternal infection is often asymptomatic while fetal effects can be devastating, including microcephaly and sometimes death. Some infants are asymptomatic at birth but later develop hearing loss, visual impairment and intellectual disability. HSV rarely causes birth defects and is usually transmitted during delivery.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Infectious agents (cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex) slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops chickenpox (varicella) at 16 weeks of gestation. According to the lecture, approximately what percentage of infants are malformed after maternal infection at this stage?
questions.explanation: About 0.4% of infants are malformed when maternal infection occurs before 13 weeks, and about 2% when it occurs at 13–20 weeks. Defects include skin scarring, limb hypoplasia, and eye and CNS defects. Infection around labour can instead cause severe neonatal infection and fatal meningoencephalitis.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Infectious agents (varicella) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A pregnant woman who keeps cats and often eats undercooked meat delivers a baby with hydrocephalus. Skull imaging shows scattered cerebral calcifications. The most likely cause is:
options: Rubella virus
Herpes simplex virus
Toxoplasma gondii
Varicella-zoster virus
questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from poorly cooked meat and from the faeces of domestic animals, especially cats. Its characteristic fetal features are cerebral calcifications and hydrocephalus. Infants who look normal at birth may later develop visual impairment, hearing loss, seizures and intellectual disability.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Infectious agents (toxoplasmosis) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which pairing of a physical agent with the birth defects it causes is correct?
options: X-rays — phocomelia (limb reduction) and heart malformations
Hyperthermia — anencephaly, spina bifida and intellectual disability
Hyperthermia — cerebral calcifications, hydrocephalus and seizures
X-rays — cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus and deafness
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia is linked to anencephaly, spina bifida and intellectual disability, and X-rays to microcephaly, spina bifida, cleft palate and limb defects. Phocomelia comes from thalidomide, calcifications with hydrocephalus from toxoplasmosis, and cataract/PDA/deafness from rubella.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Physical agents slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A baby is born with severely shortened limbs, with the hands and feet attached almost directly to the trunk (phocomelia), and a heart malformation. Which drug taken early in pregnancy is most likely responsible?
options: Phenytoin (diphenylhydantoin)
Valproic acid
Isotretinoin
Thalidomide
questions.explanation: Thalidomide, a sedative, causes limb defects, especially phocomelia, and heart malformations. Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome (facial defects, intellectual disability), and valproate mainly neural tube defects.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chemical agents (drugs) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Fetal valproate syndrome, caused by the anticonvulsant valproic acid, is characterized by:
options: Neural tube defects with heart, craniofacial and limb anomalies
Phocomelia with heart malformations as the main defects
Cerebral calcifications with hydrocephalus and later seizures
Caudal dysgenesis (sirenomelia), the 'mermaid' anomaly
questions.explanation: Valproic acid causes fetal valproate syndrome: neural tube defects plus heart, craniofacial and limb anomalies. Another anticonvulsant, phenytoin, causes fetal hydantoin syndrome (facial defects and intellectual disability). Phocomelia is from thalidomide, and caudal dysgenesis from maternal diabetes.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chemical agents (drugs) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Isotretinoin (vitamin A) embryopathy is characterized by:
options: Small, abnormally shaped ears, mandibular hypoplasia, cleft palate and heart defects
Phocomelia (severe limb reduction) with heart malformations
Cerebral calcifications, hydrocephalus and later visual impairment
Short palpebral fissures, indistinct philtrum, thin upper lip and maxillary hypoplasia
questions.explanation: Isotretinoin (vitamin A) embryopathy causes small, abnormally shaped ears, mandibular hypoplasia, cleft palate and heart defects. Phocomelia is from thalidomide, and short palpebral fissures with an indistinct philtrum and thin upper lip are features of fetal alcohol syndrome.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chemical agents (drugs: vitamin A) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: A growth-restricted newborn has short palpebral fissures, maxillary hypoplasia, an indistinct philtrum, a thin upper lip and a heart defect, and later shows intellectual disability. The most likely maternal exposure is:
options: Valproic acid
Alcohol
Organic mercury
Isotretinoin
questions.explanation: These features define fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), the severe end of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). Alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND) is the milder form within the spectrum. Organic mercury causes cerebral palsy-like neurological symptoms.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chemical agents (alcohol) slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Each of the following environmental agents is correctly paired with its effect EXCEPT:
options: Organic mercury — neurological symptoms resembling cerebral palsy
Iodine deficiency — endemic cretinism (stunted mental and physical growth)
Lead — phocomelia
Zika virus — microcephaly (congenital Zika syndrome)
questions.explanation: Lead causes growth retardation and neurological disorders. Phocomelia is the thalidomide defect, so that pairing is the exception. The others are correct: organic mercury causes CP-like neurological symptoms, iodine deficiency endemic cretinism, and Zika microcephaly.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Chemical agents (heavy metals), Infectious agents (Zika) and Nutritional deficiencies slides; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Infants of diabetic mothers have a higher risk of caudal dysgenesis (sirenomelia, the 'mermaid baby'). Altered glucose levels are thought to affect which gene that regulates dorsal mesoderm formation?
options: GOOSECOID
FGFR3
BRACHYURY
IRF6
questions.explanation: Altered glucose levels may affect BRACHYURY, which regulates dorsal mesoderm formation, and this would explain caudal dysgenesis. GOOSECOID over-expression causes dicephalus, FGFR3 skeletal dysplasia, and IRF6 Van der Woude syndrome.
questions.source: Lecture: Birth Defects (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Maternal DM slide; Langman's 15e Ch.9 (pp.130–141)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the origin of dizygotic and monozygotic twins?
options: Dizygotic: one oocyte fertilized by two sperm; monozygotic: two oocytes fertilized by one sperm
Dizygotic: two oocytes fertilized by two different sperm; monozygotic: a single zygote that gives rise to two embryos
Dizygotic: a single zygote that splits after day 13; monozygotic: two oocytes fertilized by two sperm
Both arise from a single zygote and differ only in the timing of embryonic division
questions.explanation: DZ (fraternal) twins come from two separately ovulated oocytes fertilized by two different sperm, giving two zygotes. MZ twins come from one zygote that gives rise to two embryos. Incomplete splitting after day 13 produces conjoined MZ twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — What is twinning? slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Genetically, dizygotic twins are:
options: Genetically identical, and always of the same sex
Genetically identical, but they may be of different sex
As similar as ordinary siblings, and they may be of different sex
Less similar than ordinary siblings, because they share one placenta
questions.explanation: DZ twins come from two separate zygotes, so they are no more alike genetically than ordinary siblings and can be of different sex. MZ twins are genetically identical and always the same sex.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Dizygotic (fraternal) twins slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A first-trimester ultrasound of a dizygotic twin pregnancy shows what appears to be a single placental mass. What is the chorionicity and amnionicity of this pregnancy?
options: Monochorionic–diamniotic; a single placental mass means a shared chorion
Dichorionic–diamniotic; the two placentas have fused
Monochorionic–monoamniotic; one placental mass means one chorion and one amnion
Dichorionic–monoamniotic; the amnion is shared but the chorions are separate
questions.explanation: Each DZ embryo develops its own chorion and amnion, so DZ twins are dichorionic–diamniotic: 2 chorions, 2 amnions, and 2 placentas that may stay separate or fuse. A fused DZ placenta is not a true shared (monochorionic) placenta.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Dizygotic twins slide and slide figure (summary table); Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: The incidence of dizygotic twinning is influenced by each of the following EXCEPT:
options: Maternal age at conception
A family history of twinning
Day of embryonic division
Use of assisted reproduction
questions.explanation: DZ twinning reflects the release and fertilization of two oocytes, and its incidence is influenced by maternal age, parity, family history and assisted reproduction. Timing of embryonic division determines the membranes of MZ twins and has no role in DZ twinning.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Dizygotic (fraternal) twins slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In describing a twin pregnancy, the term 'chorionicity' refers to the number of:
options: Amniotic sacs
Zygotes
Chorions (placentas)
Umbilical arteries in each cord
questions.explanation: Chorionicity is the number of chorions, which corresponds to placentas, and amnionicity is the number of amniotic sacs. Zygosity (DZ vs MZ) is a separate concept, since MZ twins can be dichorionic.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — What is twinning? slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A monozygotic embryo splits at the two-cell stage, on day 2 after fertilization. What arrangement of fetal membranes will result?
options: Monochorionic–diamniotic
Dichorionic–diamniotic
Monochorionic–monoamniotic
Conjoined twins
questions.explanation: Division on days 1–3, before the chorion forms, gives each embryo its own chorion and amnion (DCDA), often with separate placentas, just as in DZ twins. Monochorionic arrangements require later division, after the chorion has formed.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Monozygotic twinning: timing of embryonic division slides and slide figure; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A monozygotic embryo divides on about day 5–6, by splitting of the inner cell mass of the blastocyst. What is the expected arrangement of fetal membranes?
options: Monochorionic–diamniotic
Dichorionic–diamniotic
Monochorionic–monoamniotic
Dichorionic–monoamniotic
