questions.explanation: By day 5–6 the trophoblast (future chorion) has formed but the amnion has not, so the twins share one chorion and placenta but develop two amniotic sacs (MCDA). Dichorionic–monoamniotic is impossible, because the amnion forms after the chorion.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Monozygotic twinning: timing of embryonic division slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A monozygotic embryonic disc splits completely on about day 10–11, after the amniotic cavity has formed. The resulting twins will be:
options: Monochorionic–diamniotic
Monochorionic–monoamniotic
Dichorionic–diamniotic
Conjoined
questions.explanation: Complete division after the amnion forms, but before day 13, gives one chorion, one amnion and one placenta (MCMA), and these twins are at risk of cord entanglement. Incomplete separation after day 13 gives conjoined twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Monozygotic twinning: timing of embryonic division slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Conjoined twins result from:
options: Fusion of two dizygotic embryos during the first week of development
Incomplete separation of a monozygotic embryonic disc after day 13
Complete division of a monozygotic embryo on days 1–3
Fertilization of a single oocyte by two different sperm
questions.explanation: Conjoined twins result from incomplete separation of an MZ embryonic disc after day 13. They are monochorionic–monoamniotic, and their type depends on the point of union. Division on days 1–3 gives separate DCDA twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: What is the 'high-yield rule' relating the timing of monozygotic division to the fetal membranes?
options: The earlier the embryo separates, the more fetal membranes are shared
Timing of division affects the number of amnions but never the number of chorions
All monozygotic twins share a single chorion, whatever the timing of division
The later the embryo separates, the more fetal membranes are shared
questions.explanation: The later the separation, the more structures are shared: DCDA, then MCDA, then MCMA, then conjoined. Early division (days 1–3) gives separate chorions, so MZ twins are not always monochorionic.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — MZ twins: timing and membranes slide (high-yield rule); Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Ultrasound shows a dichorionic–diamniotic twin pregnancy with two fetuses of the same sex. Which conclusion about zygosity is correct?
options: The twins must be dizygotic, because monozygotic twins are always monochorionic
The twins must be monozygotic, because they are of the same sex
The twins may be either dizygotic or monozygotic (division on days 1–3)
The twins must be monozygotic, because dizygotic twins are always monochorionic
questions.explanation: MZ twins that divide on days 1–3 are DCDA, so a dichorionic pregnancy does not exclude monozygosity ('monozygotic does not automatically mean monochorionic'). DZ twins are often the same sex too, so membranes and sex alone cannot settle zygosity here.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — High-yield comparison slide ('monozygotic does not automatically mean monochorionic'); Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A second-trimester ultrasound of a twin pregnancy shows one male and one female fetus. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The twins are monozygotic and monochorionic–diamniotic, and need close monitoring for FFTS
The twins could still be monozygotic if their division occurred after day 13
The twins are monozygotic but dichorionic, because division occurred on days 1–3
The twins are dizygotic and dichorionic–diamniotic, and are not at risk of feto-fetal transfusion syndrome
questions.explanation: MZ twins are genetically identical and always the same sex, so opposite-sex twins must be DZ. DZ twins are DCDA with no true shared placenta, so FFTS, which needs monochorionic vascular connections, does not occur.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — High-yield comparison slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Why are monochorionic twins at risk of complications that dichorionic twins do not face?
options: They always share a single amniotic cavity, so their umbilical cords entangle
They are always conjoined to some degree at a point of union between them
They are dizygotic and so have unequal genetic growth potential
They share a placenta that can carry vascular connections between the circulations
questions.explanation: Monochorionic twins share one placenta, so vascular connections can link their circulations. This underlies FFTS, TAPS and IUGR from unequal sharing. Many monochorionic twins are diamniotic, so a shared amniotic cavity is not the general explanation.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Why chorion matters clinically slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Feto-fetal transfusion syndrome (FFTS) is best defined as:
options: Chronic, unequal red-cell transfer between dichorionic twins with separate placentas
Transfer of maternal blood into the fetal circulation through a defective placental barrier
Unbalanced blood flow between monochorionic twins through placental vascular anastomoses
Entanglement of the umbilical cords within a shared amniotic cavity
questions.explanation: FFTS occurs in monochorionic pregnancies with clinically significant, unbalanced placental vascular connections. Chronic unequal red-cell transfer describes TAPS, also a monochorionic complication, and cord entanglement is the specific risk of MCMA twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Why chorion matters clinically and FFTS slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In a monochorionic–diamniotic pregnancy at 20 weeks, one twin is small with very little amniotic fluid around it, while the co-twin is large and surrounded by excess fluid. The small twin is best described as the:
options: Donor twin, with oligohydramnios and IUGR
Recipient twin, with oligohydramnios and polycythemia
Donor twin, with polyhydramnios and hydrops
Recipient twin, with IUGR caused by cord entanglement
questions.explanation: In FFTS the donor twin develops oligohydramnios and IUGR. The recipient develops polyhydramnios, polycythemia and, in severe disease, heart failure and hydrops.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Feto-fetal transfusion syndrome slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In a monochorionic pregnancy complicated by feto-fetal transfusion syndrome, the recipient twin typically develops:
options: Oligohydramnios and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
Anemia, oligohydramnios and a small, 'stuck' appearance
Cord entanglement with its co-twin in a shared sac
Polyhydramnios, polycythemia, and possibly heart failure and hydrops
questions.explanation: The recipient twin receives excess blood through the placental anastomoses and develops polyhydramnios, polycythemia and, in severe disease, heart failure and hydrops. Oligohydramnios and IUGR are the features of the donor.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Feto-fetal transfusion syndrome slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Which monochorionic twin complication is defined by chronic, unequal transfer of red cells between the twins?
options: Twin anemia–polycythemia sequence (TAPS)
Umbilical cord entanglement (MCMA)
Conjoined twinning (thoracopagus)
Fusion of dizygotic placentas
questions.explanation: TAPS is chronic unequal red-cell transfer across the shared monochorionic placenta. FFTS is the broader imbalance of blood flow with donor oligohydramnios and recipient polyhydramnios. Fused DZ placentas are not truly shared and do not cause these problems.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Why chorion matters clinically slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In monochorionic twins, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) of one twin can result from:
options: Cord entanglement within a diamniotic pregnancy
Division of the embryo after day 13
Unequal sharing of the common placenta
Different genotypes, since monochorionic twins are dizygotic
questions.explanation: Monochorionic twins share one placenta, and if it is shared unequally the twin with the smaller share can develop IUGR. Monochorionic twins are monozygotic, and cord entanglement requires a shared (monoamniotic) cavity.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Why chorion matters clinically slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A twin pregnancy is diagnosed as monochorionic–monoamniotic. Besides the general monochorionic risks, which specific complication requires close monitoring?
options: Complete absence of vascular connections between the two circulations
Late division into conjoined twins during the third trimester
Development of two separate placentas
Umbilical cord entanglement, because both fetuses share one amniotic cavity
questions.explanation: MCMA twins share one amniotic cavity, so their umbilical cords can entangle, and Step 4 of the clinical approach is close monitoring for cord complications. Because they also share a chorion, vascular connections (with FFTS/TAPS risk) are present, not absent.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Why chorion matters clinically and Clinical approach slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In which twin pregnancy can feto-fetal transfusion syndrome occur?
options: Dizygotic, with fused placentas
Monozygotic, monochorionic–diamniotic
Monozygotic, dichorionic–diamniotic
Dizygotic, with two separate placentas
questions.explanation: FFTS needs a shared (monochorionic) placenta with vascular anastomoses, so it occurs only in monochorionic, and therefore monozygotic, twins. DCDA twins have no true shared placenta, whether they are DZ (even with fused placentas) or MZ split on days 1–3.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — High-yield comparison slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Ultrasound assessment of chorionicity in a twin pregnancy is most reliable when performed:
options: Early in pregnancy
In the third trimester
At term, just before delivery
At any time, since reliability does not change with gestational age
questions.explanation: Ultrasound assessment of the chorion is most reliable early in pregnancy. This is why Step 1 of the clinical approach is to determine chorionicity and amnionicity by ultrasound.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Feto-fetal transfusion syndrome slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: In conjoined twins, the type (e.g., thoracopagus, craniopagus) is determined by:
options: The number of placentas
The point of union between the twins
Whether the twins are of the same sex
The number of umbilical arteries
questions.explanation: Conjoined twins are named by the point of union: thoracopagus (thorax), omphalopagus (umbilical/abdominal region), pygopagus (sacrum/buttocks), ischiopagus (pelvis), and craniopagus (head). Shared organs may include the heart, liver, GIT or nervous system.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Conjoined twins are joined at the chest and share a heart. This type is called:
options: Craniopagus
Pygopagus
Ischiopagus
Thoracopagus
questions.explanation: Thoracopagus twins are joined at the thorax and may share the heart. Craniopagus are joined at the head, pygopagus at the sacral (buttock) region, and ischiopagus at the pelvis.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins slide and slide figure (conjoined twin drawings); Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Conjoined twins joined back to back at the sacral (buttock) region are classified as:
options: Thoracopagus
Pygopagus
Omphalopagus
Craniopagus
questions.explanation: Pygopagus twins are joined at the sacrum and buttocks (Greek pyge, rump). Omphalopagus twins are joined at the umbilical/abdominal region, and craniopagus at the head.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins slide and slide figure (conjoined twin drawings); Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Which pairing of a conjoined-twin type with its site of union is correct?
options: Ischiopagus — pelvis
Craniopagus — sacrum
Omphalopagus — head
Thoracopagus — buttocks
questions.explanation: Ischiopagus twins are joined at the pelvis (ischium), craniopagus at the head, omphalopagus at the umbilical/abdominal region, thoracopagus at the chest, and pygopagus at the sacrum/buttocks.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Conjoined twins are suspected on a routine ultrasound. According to the lecture's clinical approach, what is the appropriate next step?
options: Define shared anatomy by ultrasound and fetal MRI; refer to a multidisciplinary center
Wait until delivery, since shared anatomy cannot be assessed before birth
Assess chorionicity only, because conjoined twins are always dichorionic
Monitor for FFTS only, because conjoined twins never share organs
questions.explanation: Prenatal ultrasound and fetal MRI help define the shared anatomy (heart, liver, GIT, nervous system), and the pregnancy should go to a specialized multidisciplinary center (Step 5). Conjoined twins are monochorionic–monoamniotic.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Conjoined twins and Clinical approach slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: According to the lecture's clinical approach to a twin pregnancy, what is Step 1?
options: Monitor for umbilical cord entanglement
Refer to a multidisciplinary fetal center
Determine zygosity by DNA testing of both fetuses
Determine chorionicity and amnionicity by ultrasound
questions.explanation: Step 1 is to determine chorionicity and amnionicity by ultrasound, best done early. Step 2 establishes fetal number, viability, growth, anatomy and placental relationships, followed by targeted surveillance: FFTS/TAPS/IUGR for monochorionic twins and cord complications for monoamniotic twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Clinical approach slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: A monochorionic–diamniotic twin pregnancy has been confirmed. Surveillance should specifically target which complications?
options: Umbilical cord entanglement only
None, since each twin has its own amniotic sac
Feto-fetal transfusion syndrome, TAPS and IUGR
Conjoined twinning developing later in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Step 3 calls for monitoring monochorionic twins for FFTS, TAPS, IUGR and other complications, because they share a placenta with vascular connections. Cord entanglement is the specific extra concern for monoamniotic twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Clinical approach slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes monozygotic from dizygotic twins?
options: Monozygotic twins are genetically identical and always of the same sex
Monozygotic twins always have two separate placentas
Monozygotic twins are never monochorionic
Monozygotic twins are only as genetically similar as ordinary siblings
questions.explanation: MZ twins come from one zygote, so they are genetically identical and the same sex, whereas DZ twins are like siblings and may differ in sex. MZ twins may be dichorionic or monochorionic depending on when they divide.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — High-yield comparison slide; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)

questions.stem: Monochorionic–diamniotic twins result when a monozygotic embryo divides:
options: Before the chorion has formed
After the amnion has formed
After day 13, with incomplete separation of the embryonic disc
After the chorion has formed but before the amnion has formed
questions.explanation: MCDA twins arise when division follows formation of the chorion, so it is shared, but precedes formation of the amnion, so each twin gets its own. Division before the chorion forms gives DCDA, after the amnion forms MCMA, and incomplete separation after day 13 conjoined twins.
questions.source: Lecture: Twinning (Prof. E. Elzawawy) — Monozygotic twinning: timing of embryonic division slides; Langman's 15e Ch.8 (Twins)
